orbital.title: 3D Orbital Explorer
orbital.desc: Real hydrogen orbitals in GPU 3D, with a neural network that learns the wavefunction live.

principle.desc: An electron in an atom isn't a dot on an orbit — it's a cloud of probability. Solving the Schrödinger equation for hydrogen gives these clouds, the orbitals ψₙₗₘ. Each dot here is a place the electron is likely to be; blue and red mark where the wavefunction is positive or negative. Where the colour vanishes is a node.
principle.observe: Raising n adds shells; raising ℓ adds lobes. Nodes = n − 1 in total.

cloud.title: Orbital cloud
cloud.desc: Each dot is a sampled point where the electron is likely to be found. Blue = ψ > 0, red = ψ < 0.

cathode_ray.title: Cathode Ray Tube — Thomson
cathode_ray.desc: Deflect an electron beam with electric and magnetic fields, and let an AI measure the electron's charge-to-mass ratio e/m.
cathode_ray.hint: drag to rotate · scroll to zoom · click parts for details

principle.desc: Electrons boiled off the cathode are accelerated, then pass between charged plates (electric field, pushes up) and through magnetic coils (pushes down). Thomson tuned the two forces to cancel — a straight beam means the electric and magnetic pushes are equal, which fixes the speed. The leftover deflection then reveals the electron's charge-to-mass ratio.
principle.observe: Raise B until the beam is straight (forces balanced), then read e/m.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.vaccHelp: Speeds up the electrons (higher = faster beam).
controls.vdHelp: Electric field between the plates — deflects the beam up.
controls.bHelp: Magnetic field from the coils — deflects the beam down.

ai.title: AI — Measures e/m
ai.desc: The electron's charge-to-mass ratio is unknown. Collect noisy deflection measurements, then let gradient descent learn e/m — watch the estimate converge to the true value.
ai.how:
The unknown here is one number: the electron's charge-to-mass ratio e/m.
We feed the AI many magnetic-deflection measurements (each a bit noisy).
It starts with a wrong guess for e/m and predicts what each deflection should be.
Using gradient descent it repeatedly adjusts e/m to make its predictions match the measurements, shrinking the error each step.
The estimate slides to the true value 1.76×10¹¹ C/kg — the AI has 'measured' the constant from data.

gun.title: Electron gun
gun.desc: Heated cathode boils off electrons. They are accelerated toward the anode into a narrow beam.

plateP.title: + deflection plate
plateP.desc: Positive plate creates an upward electric force on the negative electron beam.

plateN.title: − deflection plate
plateN.desc: Negative plate completes the capacitor gap that deflects the beam.

coils.title: Magnetic coils
coils.desc: Current in the coils creates B perpendicular to the beam, pushing electrons downward.

screen.title: Phosphor screen
screen.desc: Where the beam lands. The glowing spot shows how far the beam was deflected.

beam.title: Electron beam
beam.desc: A stream of electrons. Its curvature reveals the charge-to-mass ratio e/m.

millikan.title: Millikan Oil Drop — the Elementary Charge
millikan.desc: Charged oil drops float between capacitor plates. Their charges are all multiples of one quantum — let an AI discover the elementary charge e.
millikan.hint: drag to rotate · scroll to zoom · click parts for details

principle.desc: A tiny oil drop carrying a few extra electrons hangs between two charged plates. Raising the plate voltage increases the upward electric force; when it exactly balances gravity the drop floats. Because charge comes in whole electrons, the balancing charges of many drops are all multiples of one smallest value — the elementary charge.
principle.equation: q·(V/d) = m·g    →    q = m·g·d / V    ·    q = n·e
principle.observe: Plot every drop's charge: they line up on evenly-spaced rungs. The rung spacing is e.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.voltageHelp: Electric field strength. Balances gravity when tuned to a drop's charge.
controls.noiseHelp: Scatter added to each measured charge.

ai.title: AI — Discovers the charge quantum e
ai.desc: Each drop's charge is an unknown whole-number multiple of a single quantum. The AI searches for the largest charge e that makes every measurement a multiple — the elementary charge.
ai.how:
Every drop's charge should be a whole-number multiple of one quantum e — but we don't know e.
The AI scores a candidate e by how well ALL charges land on multiples of it (a 'comb' that is zero when they line up perfectly).
It searches e from coarse to fine, keeping the value that fits best and zooming in around it.
The largest e that fits every drop is the elementary charge. This is unsupervised pattern discovery — no answer was given, the AI found the hidden quantum.

plateP.title: + plate
plateP.desc: Top capacitor plate. Positive charge pulls electrons on the drops upward when voltage is high enough.

plateN.title: − plate
plateN.desc: Bottom plate. With the top plate positive, an E field points downward between the plates.

drop.title: Oil drop
drop.desc: A tiny charged drop. Colour shows how many electron charges it carries. Motion reveals the balance voltage.

mass_spec.title: Mass Spectrometer — Isotopes
mass_spec.desc: Ions are separated by mass in a magnetic field. An AI reads the isotope pattern and identifies which element the sample is.
mass_spec.hint: toggle 2D/3D · watch ions curve by mass · AI reads the isotope fingerprint

principle.desc: The sample is ionised and accelerated to the same energy, then a magnetic field bends each ion into a semicircle. Heavier ions are harder to bend, so they travel a wider arc and land farther along the detector. The pattern of landing positions — the mass spectrum — shows each isotope's mass and abundance, a fingerprint unique to the element.
principle.observe: 2D: accelerator → velocity selector → B-field arcs → detector. Heavier isotopes swing wider; raise B or lower V shrinks every radius.

source.title: Ion source
source.desc: The sample is ionised here. Atoms lose electrons and become charged ions.

ion.title: Ion
ion.desc: A charged atom moving through the instrument. Colour shows mass — lighter = cyan, heavier = pink.

slits.title: Acceleration slits
slits.desc: Ions pass through a voltage gap and all reach the same kinetic energy before entering the magnetic field.

magnet.title: Magnetic field
magnet.desc: Bends each ion into a circular arc. Radius r ∝ √m — heavier ions swing wider.

detector.title: Detector
detector.desc: Counts where ions land. The bar heights build the mass spectrum fingerprint.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.voltageHelp: Sets the ion energy. Higher V → wider arcs.
controls.fieldHelp: Bends the ions. Higher B → tighter arcs.
controls.ionCountHelp: More ions = easier to see the mass separation.

ai.title: AI — Identifies the element
ai.desc: Each element leaves a unique isotope fingerprint. The AI matches the measured spectrum against known patterns to name the unknown sample.
ai.how:
Every element has a unique isotope 'fingerprint' — a set of peaks at particular masses with particular heights.
The AI knows the ideal fingerprint of each candidate element.
It compares the measured spectrum to each one and measures how similar they are (cosine similarity).
Those similarities become confidence percentages (softmax), and the best match is the AI's answer. This is pattern-recognition classification, the same idea behind image recognition.

cross_section.title: Effective Cross-section — Mean Free Path
cross_section.desc: Fire a particle beam through a target slab. Each collision removes a particle; the AI estimates the cross-section σ from transmission measurements.
cross_section.hint: drag to rotate · scroll to zoom · click parts for details

principle.desc: Target atoms present an effective cross-section σ. A beam particle travels in a straight line until it strikes one. Averaged over many particles, the distance before collision is the mean free path λ = 1/(nσ). The fraction transmitted through thickness L falls as exp(−L/λ).
principle.observe: Raise density or target size → more collisions, lower transmission. Compare measured λ with theory.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.densityHelp: Number of target spheres in the slab.

ai.title: AI — Estimates cross-section σ
ai.desc: Collect transmission at several target densities. The AI searches for σ that best fits T ≈ exp(−nσL).
ai.how:
Each density gives a measured transmission fraction.
The AI tries candidate values of σ and predicts T = exp(−nσL) for each density.
It keeps the σ that minimizes the squared error — discovering the hidden cross-section from attenuation data alone.

slab.title: Target slab
slab.desc: Region filled with scattering targets. Beam particles collide or pass through.

beam.title: Particle beam
beam.desc: Incoming particles fired from the left. Yellow = still moving; red flash = collision.

rutherford.title: Rutherford Scattering — the Nucleus
rutherford.desc: PhET-style 2D + 3D dual lab: plum pudding vs nuclear atom, α trajectories, θ histogram; 3D beam with click tips; AI deduces Z from N(θ).
rutherford.hint: 2D|3D · PhET-style 2D: plum pudding vs nuclear · 3D: orbit & click tips

principle.desc: Positively-charged alpha particles are repelled by the atom's positive charge. In Thomson's plum pudding model the charge is spread out — alphas barely bend. Rutherford's nuclear model concentrates charge in a tiny core — rare head-on hits bounce back. How often large angles occur reveals the nuclear charge Z.
principle.observe: Switch to Nuclear atom and Gold — watch back-scatter in the histogram. Plum pudding keeps angles small. Lower energy → more bending.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.energyHelp: Higher energy → smaller scattering angles (faster alphas).
controls.view3dHelp: 3D view: drag to orbit · scroll to zoom · click nucleus, beam, or α for scattering angle θ and impact parameter b.

rutherford.note: PhET-inspired side view. Plum pudding uses weak spread charge; nuclear model uses full Coulomb repulsion from a point nucleus.

ai.title: AI — Infers nuclear charge Z
ai.desc: The nucleus is unknown. Collect the noisy count-vs-angle distribution, then let gradient descent fit Rutherford's law N ∝ Z²/sin⁴(θ/2) to deduce the charge Z.
ai.how:
Rutherford's law says the count at each angle follows N ∝ Z²/sin⁴(θ/2) — the only unknown is the nuclear charge Z.
We give the AI the measured count-vs-angle data (with noise).
It starts from a wrong Z and, by gradient descent, adjusts Z until the predicted curve matches the data.
The estimate converges to the true Z. So from just 'how often alphas scatter to each angle', the AI deduces the charge of the nucleus — the inverse problem Rutherford solved by hand.

nucleus.title: Nucleus
nucleus.desc: Tiny dense core with charge +Z. Coulomb repulsion deflects incoming alpha particles.

alpha.title: Alpha particle
alpha.desc: Helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons), +2 charge. Most pass with small angles; rare head-on hits bounce back.

beam.title: Alpha beam
beam.desc: Stream of alpha particles fired at the foil target from the left.

planetary.title: Planetary Nuclear Model
planetary.desc: Electrons orbit a tiny nucleus. Toggle classical radiation to watch the spiral collapse.
planetary.hint: toggle radiation ON to see why classical atoms cannot be stable

principle.desc: Rutherford's scattering showed positive charge concentrated in a tiny nucleus with electrons orbiting outside — like a miniature solar system. Pure classical orbits are unstable: accelerating charges must radiate.
principle.equation: ω ∝ r^{-3/2} (Kepler-like)    ·    radiating electron loses energy → spiral
principle.observe: Radiation OFF: orbits look stable (unphysical). Radiation ON: electrons spiral inward, emitting light — atom collapses in ~10⁻¹¹ s classically.

compare.stable: Classical model without radiation: electrons stay in fixed orbits (this cannot happen in real classical EM).
compare.radiating: With Larmor radiation: accelerating charges lose energy → orbits shrink → atom collapses. Bohr fixed this with quantized orbits.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.scaleNote: Nucleus is ~10⁴× smaller than atom (not to scale here)

nucleus.title: Nucleus
nucleus.desc: Almost all mass and positive charge in a volume ~10⁴× smaller than the atom.

electron.title: Electron
electron.desc: Negative charge orbiting the nucleus. Accelerating charge radiates electromagnetic energy.

ai.title: AI — Infers orbit radius
ai.desc: Collect noisy orbital-period measurements. The AI searches the radius that best fits Kepler-like timing.
ai.how:
Orbital period depends on radius through ω ∝ r^{-1.5}.
The AI tries different radii and compares predicted periods to noisy measurements.
Grid search zooms in on the radius that minimises mismatch.

cloud_chamber.title: Cloud Chamber — Alpha Tracks
cloud_chamber.desc: Look into a diffusion cloud chamber: white condensation trails show α particles. Most go straight; rare kinks reveal a nucleus.
cloud_chamber.hint: 2D top view · Fire batch · Clear · gold flash = nuclear hit

principle.desc: A classroom diffusion cloud chamber has a cold black plate and alcohol vapour. Ionising alphas leave white droplet trails. Almost every track is straight — the atom is mostly empty. A rare sharp kink is a close encounter with a tiny nucleus.
principle.equation: Rutherford scatter: rare close hits bend +2 α away from +Z nucleus
principle.observe: Watch continuous white trails. Fire a batch of ~40 — expect a few bright gold/red bends. A gold flash marks the nucleus at the kink.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.energyHelp: Higher energy → longer tracks, fewer scatters.

ai.title: AI — Infers Z from backscatter
ai.desc: Measure the backscatter fraction from many tracks. The AI searches Z so the model fraction matches.
ai.how:
Backscatter probability grows with nuclear charge Z.
The AI measures the rare backscatter fraction and grid-searches Z until the empirical model matches — like identifying the foil element from track statistics.

foil.title: Cold plate
foil.desc: Black base cooled so alcohol vapour becomes supersaturated. White trails of droplets form on ions left by alphas.

source.title: Alpha source
source.desc: Radioactive tip emitting He²⁺ (alpha) particles into the vapour layer.

nucleus.title: Nucleus
nucleus.desc: Invisible until a close hit — then a brief flash marks where the α was deflected.

alpha.title: Alpha track
alpha.desc: Thick white condensation trail. Straight = empty atom; kink = nuclear scatter.

spectral_density.title: Spectral Energy Density
spectral_density.desc: Blackbody u(λ,T) vs wavelength. Highlight a band and read its energy fraction.
spectral_density.hint: pause to inspect · move cursor along the spectrum · click parts for details

principle.desc: Thermal radiation is described by spectral energy density u(λ,T): energy per unit volume per wavelength interval. The Planck curve is the measured blackbody spectrum.
principle.observe: Move the cursor: the shaded band shows u·dλ — energy in a narrow wavelength range.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.temperatureHelp: Hotter → brighter, peak shifts to shorter λ.
controls.cursorHelp: Centre of the highlighted wavelength band.

ai.title: AI — Infers temperature
ai.desc: Collect noisy spectral density samples. Grid-search T to fit the Planck law.
ai.how:
At each wavelength the Planck shape depends on T.
The AI tries temperatures and minimises relative error vs noisy u(λ) measurements.
Coarse-to-fine grid search converges on the true cavity temperature.

cavity.title: Blackbody cavity
cavity.desc: Hot walls emit thermal radiation at every wavelength inside.

slab.title: Aperture / sample
slab.desc: Light escaping the cavity carries the spectral energy density u(lambda,T).

bb_features.title: Features of Blackbody Radiation
bb_features.desc: Planck spectrum with Wien peak and blackbody colour — raise T and watch λ_max shift. AI infers T from the peak.
bb_features.note: Hotter → peak moves to shorter λ (Wien) and total power grows as σT⁴. The colour swatch approximates the glow.

principle.desc: A cavity with a small hole is an ideal blackbody (Kirchhoff). Planck’s law gives u(λ,T). Wien’s law λ_max = b/T shifts the peak; Stefan–Boltzmann power grows as σT⁴. Inspired by classroom blackbody spectrum labs.
principle.observe: 2D: rainbow visible band, Wien peak marker, colour orb. Raise T → peak shifts left and brightens. 3D: cavity aperture emits; the sphere shows the thermal colour.

ai.title: AI — Infers T from Wien peak
ai.desc: Measure a noisy peak wavelength. Search T using λ_max = b/T.
ai.how:
Wien's law links peak wavelength and temperature: λ_max = b/T.
The AI measures a noisy peak and grid-searches T until the predicted peak matches.

cavity.title: Hohlraum cavity
cavity.desc: Ideal blackbody — Kirchhoff: perfect absorber and emitter. Light from the aperture has the Planck spectrum.

rayleigh_jeans.title: Rayleigh–Jeans — UV Catastrophe
rayleigh_jeans.desc: Classical u ∝ 1/λ⁴ diverges in the UV. Compare with the measured Planck curve.
rayleigh_jeans.hint: toggle 2D/3D · dashed red = classical · cyan = Planck · click parts for details

principle.desc: Classical equipartition gives u = 8πkT/λ⁴, matching experiment only at long wavelengths. As λ→0 it predicts infinite energy — the ultraviolet catastrophe.
principle.observe: 2D overlay: curves agree at long λ; classical shoots up in the UV while Planck rolls over.

ai.title: AI — Infers T from spectrum
ai.desc: Noisy Planck spectral samples at unknown T. Grid-search to fit the blackbody shape.
ai.how:
Only the Planck curve matches the measured short-wavelength roll-off.
The AI fits noisy u(λ) data by searching temperature — the inverse blackbody problem.

cavity.title: Rayleigh–Jeans region
cavity.desc: Classical equipartition predicts u grows as lambda^-4 — UV catastrophe.

planetary_disadvantages.title: Disadvantages of the Planetary Model
planetary_disadvantages.desc: Three classical failures: radiative collapse, continuous spectra, no stable radius.
planetary_disadvantages.hint: pause to inspect · switch problem with chips · click parts for details

principle.desc: Rutherford's nuclear model places electrons in classical orbits, but electrodynamics predicts radiative collapse, continuous emission spectra, and no preferred orbit size — all wrong for real atoms.
principle.equation: accelerating charge radiates → spiral    ·    any r allowed → continuous spectrum
principle.observe: Step through radiation, spectrum, and stability animations.

verdict.spectrum: Predicts rainbow; atoms emit sharp lines
verdict.stability: No reason for one radius over another

notes.radiation: An orbiting electron accelerates and must radiate electromagnetic energy, spiraling inward.
notes.spectrum: Any orbit radius is allowed → all wavelengths. Hydrogen emits discrete lines only.
notes.stability: Classical mechanics allows infinitely many orbit sizes with no energy selection rule.

ai.title: AI — Infers collapse rate
ai.desc: From noisy energy-decay samples during radiative collapse, estimate the classical loss rate.
ai.how:
Classical radiation drains orbital energy at some rate.
The AI fits E(t) ≈ 100 − rate·t to noisy samples and grid-searches the decay rate.

nucleus.title: Nucleus
nucleus.desc: Classical model fails: radiating electrons should spiral inward.

planck.title: Planck's Law — Quantum Radiation
planck.desc: A glowing cavity follows Planck's law — shrink h toward zero and the classical Rayleigh–Jeans catastrophe returns. An AI measures h from the spectrum.
planck.hint: drag to rotate · scroll to zoom · click cavity for details

principle.desc: Classical physics predicted infinite energy at short wavelengths (the ultraviolet catastrophe). Planck fixed it by assuming energy is exchanged in quanta E = hν. The Planck spectrum matches experiment; as h → 0 it collapses to the divergent Rayleigh–Jeans curve.
principle.observe: Raise temperature → peak shifts to shorter λ. Lower h scale → Planck curve approaches classical (diverges in UV).

controls.title: Parameters
controls.temperatureHelp: Hotter → brighter, peak at shorter wavelength.

ai.title: AI — Measures Planck's constant h
ai.desc: Collect noisy spectral density measurements at known T. The AI searches for h that best fits the Planck law.
ai.how:
At fixed temperature, the Planck spectral shape depends on h.
The AI tries different values of h and compares predicted u(λ,T) to noisy measurements.
It adjusts h until the Planck curve matches — measuring the quantum of action from blackbody data.

cavity.title: Blackbody cavity
cavity.desc: An ideal radiator. Its colour and spectrum depend only on temperature.

photoelectric.title: Photoelectric Effect — the Quantum of Light
photoelectric.desc: AllVisualizer-style lab: coloured photons hit a metal. Electrons leave only if hf ≥ φ. Intensity raises the rate, not KE_max. AI measures h from V_s vs f.
photoelectric.hint: 2D metal surface · raise frequency past threshold · intensity = more electrons · try stopping voltage

principle.desc: Light comes in packets (photons) of energy E = hf. One photon frees at most one electron, and only if it carries more than the metal's work function φ. Below threshold frequency nothing happens no matter how bright the light — brightness only adds more photons. Above threshold, KE_max = hf − φ, which a reverse stopping voltage can cancel.
principle.observe: 2D: photons strike the metal plate; green flash = ejection. Readout shows hf, φ, f₀, KE_max. Bottom plot is Einstein KE vs f. 3D: tube view of the same physics.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.freqHelp: Photon energy = h·f. Below threshold → no electrons.
controls.intensityHelp: More photons per second → more ejected electrons, same max KE (quantum signature).
controls.vstopHelp: Reverse voltage that opposes the electrons; halts them when V_s ≥ KE.

ai.title: AI — Measures Planck's constant h
ai.desc: Collect stopping voltage V_s at several frequencies, then let the AI fit the line V_s = (h/e)·f − φ/e. Its slope gives h.
ai.how:
Einstein's relation makes the stopping voltage a straight line in frequency: V_s = (h/e)·f − φ/e.
The AI is given noisy (frequency, stopping-voltage) points.
By gradient descent it adjusts the line's slope and intercept to best fit the points.
The slope equals h/e, so the fitted slope yields Planck's constant h, and the intercept gives the work function φ. A fundamental constant, measured by fitting a line to data.

source.title: Light source
source.desc: Emits photons at the chosen frequency. Higher frequency = more energetic light quanta.

cathode.title: Cathode (metal)
cathode.desc: Metal surface with work function φ. Electrons need hf ≥ φ to escape.

anode.title: Anode
anode.desc: Collects photoelectrons. A stopping voltage can turn them back before they arrive.

photon.title: Photon
photon.desc: Light quantum with energy E = hf. Colour indicates frequency.

electron.title: Photoelectron
electron.desc: Electron ejected when a photon delivers enough energy to overcome the work function.

wave_theory.title: Wave Theory vs Photoelectric Effect
wave_theory.desc: Classical wave predictions for the photoelectric effect are wrong on all three counts — compare them side by side with experiment and let an AI discover h.

principle.desc: Classical wave theory says electron energy should grow with light intensity, any frequency should work if bright enough, and dim light needs time to accumulate energy. Experiment shows KE depends only on frequency, there is a threshold, and emission is instantaneous.
principle.equation: Classical: KE ∝ I    ·    Quantum: KE_max = hν − W
principle.observe: Raise intensity — classical bar grows, quantum bar unchanged. Raise frequency past threshold — electrons appear instantly.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.frequencyHelp: Photon energy E = hν. Below threshold → no electrons.
controls.intensityHelp: Classical theory ties KE to brightness; experiment does not.

ai.title: AI — Discovers Planck constant h
ai.desc: Collect noisy KE_max measurements at several frequencies. The AI searches for h that best fits KE = hν − W.
ai.how:
On the experimental side, KE_max = hν − W is a straight line in frequency.
The AI receives noisy (frequency, KE) points from above-threshold measurements.
It scores candidate values of h by how well they predict each KE.
A coarse-to-fine grid search narrows h until the estimate converges to Planck's constant.

plateN.title: Classical metal plate
plateN.desc: Wave theory: continuous energy delivery — no threshold frequency.

plateP.title: Quantum plate
plateP.desc: Energy arrives in quanta hf — explains photoelectric threshold.

quantum_theory.title: Quantum Theory — Photons & the Photoelectric Effect
quantum_theory.desc: Light arrives as photons E = hν. One photon frees one electron: KE_max = hν − W. An AI discovers h from the KE vs frequency line.

principle.desc: Einstein's photon model: each photon carries energy hν and can free at most one electron. Below the threshold frequency ν₀ = W/h, no electrons emerge regardless of intensity. Plotting KE_max vs ν gives a line of slope h.
principle.observe: Switch metal to change W. Below threshold: photons arrive but no electrons. Above: instant ejection.

ai.title: AI — Discovers Planck constant h
ai.desc: Collect noisy KE_max vs frequency data. Grid search finds h in KE = hν − W.
ai.how:
Einstein's relation makes KE_max a linear function of frequency with slope h/e.
The AI tries different values of h and scores how well each predicts the noisy KE measurements.
Grid search from coarse to fine homes in on Planck's constant.

plateN.title: Metal surface
plateN.desc: Electrons bound by work function phi — need hf > phi to escape.

source.title: UV light source
source.desc: Einstein: one photon gives all its energy to one electron.

applications.title: Applications of the Photoelectric Effect
applications.desc: Photomultiplier tubes amplify single photons through dynode cascades; solar cells convert light directly to electricity. An AI discovers the secondary emission factor δ.
applications.hint: switch device · watch one photon become thousands (PMT) or e⁻/h⁺ pairs (solar)

principle.desc: A PMT: one photon frees one electron at the photocathode; each dynode emits δ secondary electrons, so gain ≈ δ^N. A solar cell: photons at a p-n junction create e-h pairs swept to contacts, driving current through a load.
principle.equation: PMT gain ≈ δ^N    ·    Solar: I ∝ light intensity
principle.observe: PMT: green photon → 1 electron → δ at each dynode → huge pulse at anode. Solar: more sunlight → more carriers → higher µA.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.dynodesHelp: More stages → gain grows as δ^N (exponential).
controls.secondaryHelp: Electrons emitted per impact at each dynode.
controls.intensityHelp: More photons → more e⁻/h⁺ pairs and current.

compare.pmt: PMT: ONE photon triggers a cascade — each dynode multiplies electrons by δ. Total gain ≈ δ^N.
compare.solar: Solar cell: photons create electron–hole pairs at the p-n junction. Carriers separate → current through the load.

photocathode.title: Photocathode
photocathode.desc: One photon ejects one photoelectron (photoelectric effect).

dynode.title: Dynode stage
dynode.desc: Each impacting electron knocks out ~δ secondary electrons (secondary emission).

anode.title: Anode
anode.desc: Collects the amplified electron pulse — one photon became δ^N electrons.

lamp.title: Sunlight
lamp.desc: Photons carry energy to the solar cell; intensity sets carrier rate.

pSide.title: p-type layer
pSide.desc: Holes (h⁺) are the majority carriers; photogenerated h⁺ drift this way.

nSide.title: n-type layer
nSide.desc: Electrons are majority carriers; photogenerated e⁻ drift this way.

junction.title: p-n junction
junction.desc: Internal field separates photogenerated e⁻ and h⁺ — no battery needed.

load.title: External load
load.desc: Current flows through the circuit — light converted to usable electricity.

ai.title: AI — Discovers secondary emission δ
ai.desc: Collect noisy gain vs dynode-count measurements. Grid search finds δ in gain = δ^N.
ai.how:
PMT gain grows as δ raised to the number of dynodes.
The AI receives noisy (N, gain) measurements.
It scores candidate δ values by how well δ^N matches each gain.
Grid search converges on the secondary emission factor.

frank_hertz.title: Frank–Hertz — Quantized Excitation
frank_hertz.desc: Accelerate electrons through a gas-filled tube. Current dips at E₀, 2E₀, 3E₀ prove atomic energy levels are quantized — let an AI discover E₀.
frank_hertz.hint: drag to rotate · scroll to zoom · click parts for details

principle.desc: Electrons boiled off the cathode are accelerated toward a collector through low-pressure gas. When an electron's kinetic energy reaches the first excitation energy E₀, inelastic collisions drain energy and fewer electrons arrive — a dip in current. Repeating dips at multiples of E₀ prove quantization.
principle.equation: KE = e·V    ·    dips at V = n·E₀/e
principle.observe: Sweep voltage and watch I–V dips line up at E₀, 2E₀, … Switch gas to see a different E₀.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.voltageHelp: Electron energy rises with V. Dips appear when KE crosses n·E₀.

ai.title: AI — Discovers excitation energy E₀
ai.desc: Collect a noisy I–V curve. The AI searches for E₀ whose dip pattern best matches the data.
ai.how:

principle.observe: Start with Hot solid — smooth rainbow on screen. Switch to Hydrogen — only bright lines remain.

hydrogen_spectrum.title: Hydrogen Atomic Spectrum — Rydberg Formula
hydrogen_spectrum.desc: Balmer, Lyman, and Paschen series follow 1/λ = R_H(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²). An AI discovers the Rydberg constant R_H from line wavelengths.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.upperLevelHelp: Electron drops from n₂ to the series ground level n₁.

ai.title: AI — Discovers Rydberg constant R_H
ai.desc: Collect noisy Balmer-line wavelengths. Grid search finds R_H minimizing mismatch across all lines.
ai.how:
Each spectral line wavelength is fixed by the Rydberg formula with one unknown scale factor R_H.
The AI receives noisy wavelength measurements for several Balmer transitions.
It scores candidate R_H values by relative wavelength error across all lines.
Grid search converges on the Rydberg constant from spectroscopy alone.

compton.title: Compton Effect — Photon Momentum
compton.desc: X-rays scatter off electrons with a wavelength shift Δλ = λ_C(1−cos θ). An AI measures the Compton wavelength λ_C from shift data.
compton.hint: drag to rotate · scroll to zoom · click parts for details

principle.desc: When an X-ray photon collides with a nearly free electron, the scattered photon emerges at angle θ with a longer wavelength. The shift Δλ = (h/mc)(1−cos θ) depends only on θ — proving photons carry momentum, not just energy.
principle.observe: Larger scattering angle → bigger Δλ. Shift is independent of initial wavelength.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.angleHelp: Angle between incident and scattered photon.

ai.title: AI — Measures Compton wavelength λ_C
ai.desc: Collect noisy Δλ measurements at several angles. The AI fits Δλ = λ_C·(1−cos θ) to find λ_C.
ai.how:
Compton's formula is linear in (1−cos θ) with slope λ_C.
The AI receives noisy shift measurements at different angles.
By gradient descent it adjusts the slope until predicted shifts match the data — measuring h/(m_e c) from scattering alone.

electron.title: Electron
electron.desc: Nearly free electron at rest before collision.

scattered.title: Scattered photon
scattered.desc: Emerges at angle θ with longer wavelength λ' = λ + Δλ.

recoil.title: Recoil electron
recoil.desc: Electron absorbs momentum and kinetic energy from the collision.

xray_discovery.title: Discovery of X-Rays — Röntgen
xray_discovery.desc: Electrons accelerated in a high-voltage tube produce penetrating X-rays. Duane–Hunt cutoff λ_min = hc/V — let an AI discover hc from tube data.
xray_discovery.hint: pause to freeze · adjust tube voltage and intensity · click parts for details
xray_discovery.note: λ_min = hc / (eV) — higher voltage → shorter wavelength → more penetrating

principle.desc: Röntgen (1895) found that cathode-ray tubes made nearby screens glow through opaque wrapping. Electrons striking a metal target produce bremsstrahlung X-rays whose shortest wavelength is set by the tube voltage.
principle.observe: Raise voltage → shorter λ_min and harder, more penetrating X-rays.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.voltageHelp: Accelerating potential in kV. Sets maximum photon energy and cutoff wavelength.
controls.intensityHelp: Electron beam current — more electrons → more X-rays.

ai.title: AI — Discovers hc (keV·nm)
ai.desc: Collect noisy (V, λ_min) measurements from X-ray tubes. The AI finds hc in λ_min = hc/V.

Duane–Hunt says the shortest X-ray wavelength depends only on tube voltage: λ_min = hc/V.

It scores candidate hc values and searches from coarse to fine until hc converges — measuring the photon constant from bremsstrahlung alone.

cathode.title: Cathode
cathode.desc: Cold cathode emits electrons when struck — start of the discharge.

anode.title: Target (anode)

detector.title: Detector
detector.desc: Photographic plate or counter records the X-ray beam.

xray_wave.title: Wave Property of X-Rays — Bragg Diffraction
xray_wave.desc: X-rays interfere from crystal planes. Bragg's law nλ = 2d sin θ — watch constructive peaks and let an AI discover plane spacing d.
xray_wave.hint: 2D|3D · tune λ, d, θ · pause freezes beams · click 3D parts for details
xray_wave.note: Constructive when path difference δ = 2d sin θ equals an integer number of wavelengths (nλ). Classic crystallography condition.

principle.desc: X-rays reflect from regularly spaced crystal planes. The extra path from the deeper plane is 2d sin θ. When that equals nλ, reflected waves are in phase — Bragg diffraction — proof that X-rays are waves (OSP Bragg's Law style).
principle.equation: nλ = 2d sin θ    ·    δ = 2d sin θ
principle.observe: 2D: two rays + wavefronts; green I(θ) peaks at Bragg angles. 3D: detector glows when constructive. Try λ=100 pm, d=200 pm, θ=30° (n=2).

controls.title: Parameters
controls.wavelengthHelp: Wavelength in picometres (comparable to atomic spacing).
controls.angleHelp: Angle between incident beam and the crystal planes.

ai.title: AI — Discovers crystal spacing d
ai.desc: Collect noisy Bragg measurements (n, λ, θ). The AI finds d in nλ = 2d sin θ.
ai.how:
Bragg's law links wavelength, angle, and plane spacing.
The AI receives noisy path-difference measurements at various (n, λ, θ).
It searches for d that best reproduces the Bragg condition across all points.

crystal.title: Crystal planes
crystal.desc: Parallel atomic planes separated by d. Specular reflection plus interference produces Bragg peaks — wave nature of X-rays.

source.title: X-ray source
source.desc: Monochromatic beam of wavelength λ. Comparable to d so diffraction is visible.

detector.title: Detector
detector.desc: Lights up when nλ = 2d sin θ — constructive interference.

xray_particle.title: Particle Property of X-Rays — Photons
xray_particle.desc: keV X-rays arrive as photons E = hc/λ. One photon can eject one photoelectron — let an AI discover hc.
xray_particle.hint: pause to freeze · raise energy above binding energy to eject electrons · click parts for details

principle.desc: Hard X-rays behave as discrete photons. When E_photon exceeds a shell binding energy, one photon ejects at most one photoelectron: E = W + KE.
principle.observe: Below binding energy: photons arrive but no electrons. Above: discrete ejection events.

ai.title: AI — Discovers hc (keV·nm)
ai.desc: Collect noisy (E, λ) photon measurements. The AI finds hc in E = hc/λ.
ai.how:
Photon energy and wavelength are linked by hc.
The AI receives noisy energy–wavelength pairs from X-ray photons.
Grid search finds hc that best satisfies E = hc/λ for every measurement.

electron.title: Target electrons
electron.desc: Compton scattering: photon collides with electron like a particle collision.

bohr.title: Bohr's Atomic Model
bohr.desc: Electrons sit on fixed circular orbits (n = 1, 2, 3…). Click a hydrogen spectral line to watch the electron jump down and emit a photon.
bohr.hint: drag to rotate · scroll to zoom · click a spectral line below to see the jump

principle.desc: Bohr kept Rutherford's nucleus but added quantization: only certain orbits are allowed (principal quantum number n). The electron does not radiate while on one orbit. When it jumps from a higher level n₂ to a lower n₁, it emits one photon whose wavelength is fixed by the Rydberg formula.
principle.equation: r_n = n² a₀    ·    E_n = −13.6/n² eV    ·    1/λ = R_H(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²)
principle.observe: Click a spectral line or change n — the electron jumps orbits and a photon flies out. Match lines to ΔE = hf.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.nHelp: Higher n → wider orbit, electron less tightly bound (less negative energy).

info.meaningText: Each ring is an allowed stationary orbit. Only these sizes exist — not any radius in between.

chart.linesHelp: Click a line to play the transition. Hα is the famous red line (3 → 2).

ai.title: AI — Measures Rydberg constant R_H
ai.desc: Collect measured hydrogen line wavelengths. The AI finds R_H that makes every line fit 1/λ = R_H(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²).
ai.how:
Each spectral line corresponds to a transition between Bohr levels.
The Rydberg formula links wavelength to the level numbers — R_H is the only scale factor.
The AI searches for R_H that minimizes mismatch across all measured lines, discovering the constant from spectroscopy alone.

electron.title: Electron
electron.desc: Moves on a quantized circular orbit without radiating.

light_duality.title: Wave–Particle Duality of Light
light_duality.desc: lookang-style double slit: wave fringes, photon hits that build interference, or which-path detectors that destroy it. Tune λ and slit separation; AI discovers h from E = hν.

principle.desc: Light is neither purely wave nor purely particle. Unobserved photons through a double slit build an interference pattern (wave). Detecting which slit each photon took (which-path) destroys the fringes (particle). Complementarity — inspired by the lookang / EJS Double Slit Wave Particle Duality model.
principle.equation: Wave: I ∝ cos²(δ)    ·    Particle: E = hν    ·    Observe path → no fringes
principle.observe: 2D and 3D: source → slits → screen. Wave mode shows continuous fringes. Photons mode: discrete hits sample the interference probability. Which-path: red detectors → two clumps, no fringes. Change λ or slit separation d to reshape I(y).

controls.title: Parameters
controls.frequencyHelp: Sets wavelength (fringe spacing) and photon energy E = hν.
controls.intensityHelp: More photons per second in Photons / Which-path modes; brighter fringes in Wave mode.

info.which_pathEvidence: which-path detectors collapse the wave picture

canvas.particleNote: hits build the same pattern one photon at a time
canvas.complement: both wave and particle descriptions are required

ai.title: AI — Discovers Planck constant h
ai.desc: Collect noisy photon-energy vs frequency measurements. Grid search finds h in E = hν — the particle side of duality.
ai.how:
In the particle picture, photon energy is E = hν — one constant links every frequency.
The AI receives noisy (ν, E) measurements.
It scores candidate h values by how well hν matches each energy.
Grid search converges on Planck's constant.

source.title: Light source
source.desc: Coherent source. Frequency sets λ and photon energy E = hν.

slits.title: Double slit
slits.desc: Two paths. Unobserved: amplitudes interfere. Observed which-path: fringes vanish.

screen.title: Detection screen
screen.desc: Bright bands = high probability. In Photons mode, hits accumulate into fringes.

light_duality.hint: 2D|3D · Wave / Photons / Which-path · tune λ and d · pause freezes

de_broglie.title: de Broglie Matter Waves
de_broglie.desc: Every moving particle has wavelength λ = h/p. Plot λ vs speed or energy (MatterWaveX-style), watch the matter wave, and let an AI discover h.
de_broglie.hint: 2D|3D · pick particle · Velocity or KE · non-rel / rel · pause freezes the wave
de_broglie.note: λ = h/p. Faster or heavier → shorter λ. Relativistic mode uses p = γmv (MatterWaveX-style).

principle.desc: de Broglie (1924): every particle with momentum p has wavelength λ = h/p. Electrons at eV energies have atomic-sized λ — the basis of diffraction and electron microscopy. This plotter mirrors MatterWaveX: choose particle, velocity or kinetic energy, non-relativistic or relativistic.
principle.observe: 2D: traveling matter wave + λ(v) or λ(E) curve (green marker = now). 3D: particle rides a glowing wave ribbon; yellow ticks mark one λ. Switch Electron → Fullerene C₆₀ — λ collapses.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.velocityHelp: Higher speed → larger p → shorter de Broglie wavelength.
controls.energyHelp: Sets v = √(2E/m). Higher E → shorter λ.

ai.title: AI — Discovers Planck constant h
ai.desc: Collect noisy wavelength measurements at different speeds. The AI finds h that best satisfies λ = h/p for every point.
ai.how:
de Broglie says λ and p are linked by one constant: h.
For each measurement the AI predicts λ = h/p and scores how well h explains all points.
It searches from coarse to fine until h converges to Planck's constant — without being told the value.

particle.title: Particle
particle.desc: Localized mass m moving with momentum p. The glowing ribbon is its de Broglie matter wave λ = h/p.

uncertainty_et.title: ΔE Δt ≥ ħ/2
uncertainty_et.desc: Short-lived excited states have broad spectral lines. Watch decay and linewidth track the energy–time uncertainty relation — let an AI discover ħ.
uncertainty_et.hint: pause to inspect · shorter lifetime → broader line · click parts for details

principle.desc: A short-lived excited state (lifetime τ ≈ Δt) cannot have a sharp energy. The natural linewidth Γ ≈ ħ/τ (or ΔE ≈ ħ/2τ) widens as τ shortens — the energy–time uncertainty relation.
principle.observe: Shorten τ: the decay curve dies faster and the Lorentzian spectrum gets wider.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.lifetimeHelp: Excited-state lifetime in femtoseconds. Shorter τ → larger ΔE.

uncertainty_et.note: Natural linewidth of atomic transitions follows this bound.

ai.title: AI — Discovers ħ
ai.desc: Collect noisy (τ, ΔE) pairs from spectral measurements. The AI finds ħ that best satisfies ΔE ≈ ħ/2τ.
ai.how:
Energy–time uncertainty links lifetime and linewidth: ΔE ≈ ħ/2τ.
The AI scores a candidate ħ by how well it predicts every measured ΔE from τ.
Coarse-to-fine grid search narrows until ħ converges to ħ in eV·s.

packet.title: Time envelope (Delta t)
packet.desc: Short-lived pulse in time has broad energy spread Delta E.

photon.title: Energy pulse
photon.desc: Heisenberg: Delta E Delta t >= hbar/2.

wave_particle_probability.title: Wave–Particle & Probability
wave_particle_probability.desc: Polytechnique-style ψ(x) and φ(p): phase-coloured packet, |ψ|², and Born-rule detections. AI fits packet width σ.
wave_particle_probability.hint: ψ / |ψ|² / Detections · watch φ(p) on top · pause freezes phase

principle.desc: Like the École Polytechnique free-wavepacket lab: momentum φ(p) sits above position ψ(x). Colour is quantum phase. Born rule: you never see ψ itself — detections sample |ψ|² one hit at a time.
principle.observe: Widen σ: |ψ| spreads in x while φ(p) narrows. Switch to Detections — random dots rebuild the |ψ|² envelope.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.widthHelp: Gaussian width. Larger σ → wider in x, narrower in p.
controls.rateHelp: How fast random detections fire in Detections view.

notes.prob: Area under |ψ|² is the chance of finding the particle in an interval.
notes.detect: Each amber dot is one measurement. Many hits reproduce |ψ|² — the Born rule.

ai.title: AI — Discovers packet width σ
ai.desc: Collect random detection positions. The AI finds σ whose Gaussian |ψ|² best matches the hit distribution.
ai.how:
Born's rule says the hit density follows |ψ|² ∝ exp(−x²/σ²).
The AI compares a histogram of detections to candidate Gaussians.
Grid search on σ converges to the packet width that best explains the ensemble.

wave.title: ψ(x) packet
wave.desc: Position-space wavefunction. Phase colour matches the wheel; only |ψ|² is measured.

particle.title: Detection
particle.desc: One measurement finds the particle at a single x drawn from |ψ|².

wavefunction_stats.title: Wavefunction Statistics
wavefunction_stats.desc: Born rule in a 1-D box: 2D shows ψ / |ψ|² charts; 3D is a measurement chamber where detections fall onto a detector. AI discovers box width a.
wavefunction_stats.hint: 2D charts · 3D chamber · fire detections · raise n

principle.desc: Born rule: each measurement finds the particle at one random x. After many detections the histogram converges to |ψ_n(x)|². 2D is the Wavefiz-style plot; 3D is a chamber — glowing lobes mark likely regions, amber hits fall and stack on the detector.
principle.observe: 2D: toggle ψ ↔ |ψ|² and watch amber bars fill the cyan curve. 3D: fire detections — spheres rain into the bright lobes and build the same pattern.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.levelHelp: Energy level of the particle in the box (changes node count).

wavefunction_stats.note: Individual detections are random; the ensemble reveals |ψ|².

ai.title: AI — Discovers box width a
ai.desc: Use detection positions to find the well width a that makes the theoretical |ψ_n|² match the histogram.
ai.how:
For a particle in a box, |ψ_n|² depends on the width a.
The AI scores candidate widths by how well ψ_n(x,a) explains the hit histogram.
Grid search narrows a until the box size converges.

grid.title: Infinite well walls
grid.desc: V = ∞ — ψ must be zero at the boundaries.

wave.title: Detector & |ψ|² lobes
wave.desc: Cyan lobes are where |ψ|² is large. Amber spheres are individual position measurements stacking on the detector.

double_slit.title: Double-Slit Interference
double_slit.desc: Two slits produce fringes I ∝ cos²(πdy/λL). Tune λ, d, and L — let an AI discover slit separation from fringe-spacing data.
double_slit.hint: toggle 2D/3D · pause · watch fringes and the I(y) plot · click parts for details

principle.desc: A coherent wave hits two slits and interferes on a far screen. Bright fringes: path difference ≈ mλ. Dark fringes: path difference ≈ (m+½)λ. Fringe spacing Δy = λL/d — change λ, d, or L and watch the I(y) plot.
principle.observe: 2D and 3D both show source → slits → wavefronts → screen fringes + I(y). Widen d → fringes squeeze; raise λ → fringes spread.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.frequencyHelp: Higher frequency → shorter wavelength → tighter fringes.
controls.distanceHelp: Distance from slits to detection screen.

ai.title: AI — Discovers slit separation d
ai.desc: Collect noisy fringe-spacing measurements. The AI finds d from Δy = λL/d.
ai.how:
Fringe spacing Δy = λL/d links wavelength, distance, and slit separation.
For each measurement the AI predicts Δy from a candidate d.
Grid search converges to the slit separation that best fits all data.

source.title: Coherent source
source.desc: Single wavelength — needed for stable interference.

slits.title: Two slits
slits.desc: Path difference creates constructive and destructive interference.

schrodinger_discovery.title: Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation
schrodinger_discovery.desc: Numerically evolve ψ(x,t) in 1D — choose a potential and initial state, watch |ψ| and phase, and see probability flow.
schrodinger_discovery.hint: Run / Pause · Reset · try barrier + Gaussian to see tunneling · colours = phase

principle.desc: The time-dependent Schrödinger equation predicts how the complex wavefunction ψ(x,t) evolves. Height of the curve is |ψ|; colour is the phase arg(ψ). Grey background is the potential V(x). Hard walls at the edges keep the particle in 0 < x < 1.

controls.title: Simulator
controls.potentialHelp: Shape of the energy landscape the particle feels.

ai.title: AI — Discovers box width a
ai.desc: Collect quantised energy levels E_n. The AI finds a from E_n = n²π²ħ²/(2ma²).
ai.how:
Energies in a box scale as E_n ∝ n²/a².
Given noisy E_n measurements the AI scores candidate widths by how well they reproduce every level.
Grid search on a converges to the true box size.

cavity.title: Potential V(x)
cavity.desc: Grey curve — the particle feels this energy landscape.

wave.title: Time evolution
wave.desc: Schrödinger equation pushes ψ forward in time.

infinite_well.title: Infinite Square Well
infinite_well.desc: Schroeder-style well: superpose n=1…8, watch phasors rotate, and see Re/Im or |ψ|². AI discovers well width a.
infinite_well.hint: 2D|3D · click clocks · Zero / Normalize · toggle Re/Im vs |ψ|²

ai.title: AI — Discovers well width a

Each level energy depends on the box width: E_n = n²π²ℏ²/(2ma²).
