davisson_germer.title: Davisson–Germer — Electron Diffraction
davisson_germer.desc: Electrons scatter from a Ni crystal with intensity peaks at Bragg angles. λ = h/√(2meV) — let an AI discover crystal spacing d.
davisson_germer.hint: 2D|3D · sweep V and θ for peaks · pause freezes the beam · click 3D parts for details
davisson_germer.note: Surface grating: nλ = D sin θ   ·   Ni row spacing D ≈ {d} pm   ·   peak near 50° at V ≈ 54 V

principle.desc: Davisson and Germer (1927) fired low-energy electrons at a nickel crystal and observed diffraction peaks — proof that electrons are matter waves. Intensity spikes when nλ = D sin θ (surface grating), matching de Broglie λ = h/√(2meV).
principle.equation: λ = h/√(2meV)    ·    nλ = D sin θ
principle.observe: 2D: apparatus + I(θ) curve — green marker is your detector. 3D: watch electrons scatter; detector glows at a Bragg peak. At V ≈ 54 V the first peak is near θ ≈ 50° (Ni D ≈ 218 pm).

controls.title: Parameters
controls.angleHelp: Scattering angle measured from the surface.

ai.title: AI — Discovers crystal spacing d
ai.desc: Collect noisy (V, peak θ) diffraction data. The AI finds d in sin θ = nλ/d.
ai.how:
Each diffraction peak links electron wavelength (from V) to scattering angle via Bragg's law.
The AI receives noisy peak-angle measurements at different voltages.
It searches for d that best satisfies nλ = d sin θ — discovering the Ni lattice spacing from electron waves alone.

gun.title: Electron gun
gun.desc: Accelerates electrons; V sets de Broglie λ = h/√(2meV). Classic peak near 54 V.

crystal.title: Ni crystal
crystal.desc: Surface atom rows (D ≈ 218 pm) act as a diffraction grating: nλ = D sin θ.

detector.title: Detector
detector.desc: Counts scattered electrons. Bright when θ hits a diffraction peak.

wave_beam.title: Wave Beam — Matter-Wave Packet
wave_beam.desc: Localized matter-wave packet: Re(ψ) rides inside |ψ|², drifts with momentum, and spreads with dispersion. AI discovers Δk ∝ 1/Δx.
wave_beam.hint: 2D|3D · Width / Momentum / Dispersion · pause freezes the packet
wave_beam.note: Narrower width → larger Δk. Higher momentum → faster drift and tighter ripples. Dispersion spreads the packet over time.

principle.desc: A localized particle is a wave packet: carrier oscillations (Re ψ) inside a Gaussian envelope (|ψ|²). Width sets Δx, momentum sets drift and λ, dispersion makes the packet spread — as in physics-simulations.org wave-packet demos.
principle.observe: 2D: cyan Re(ψ) above purple |ψ|². 3D: phase-coloured Re/Im ribbon over a |ψ|² glow. Narrow width → Δk rises.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.widthHelp: Initial envelope width Δx. Narrower → larger Δk.
controls.momentumHelp: Mean momentum ⟨p⟩ — controls drift speed and carrier wavelength.
controls.dispersionHelp: How fast the packet spreads while propagating.

ai.title: AI — Discovers Δk = k/(2Δx)
ai.desc: Collect noisy (σ, Δk) measurements from wave packets. The AI finds k ≈ 0.5 in Δk = k/Δx.
ai.how:
A Gaussian packet has Δk inversely proportional to its width Δx.
The AI receives noisy spread measurements at different envelope widths.
Grid search finds the constant k in Δk = k/(2Δx).

source.title: Wave source
source.desc: Aperture launching the matter-wave packet. Momentum sets how fast it drifts.

uncertainty_xp.title: Heisenberg Uncertainty — Position & Momentum
uncertainty_xp.desc: Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2. Matched |ψ(x)|² and |φ(p)|² — narrow one, the other widens. An AI discovers ħ from the product.
uncertainty_xp.hint: 2D|3D · slide σₓ and momentum excess · watch the product stay ≥ ℏ/2

principle.desc: Heisenberg (1927): you cannot know position and momentum sharply at once. A Gaussian packet saturates Δx·Δp = ℏ/2. Narrowing |ψ(x)|² forces |φ(p)|² to broaden — the Fourier width trade-off taught in PhysSandbox-style labs.
principle.observe: Shrink σₓ → position peak narrows, momentum peak widens. Raise momentum excess → product climbs above ℏ/2.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.excessHelp: Multiplies σₚ above the minimum σₚ = ℏ/(2σₓ). 1× = minimum-uncertainty packet.

ai.title: AI — Discovers Planck constant ħ
ai.desc: Collect noisy Δx·Δp product measurements. The AI finds ħ from the minimum ħ/2.
ai.how:
For a Gaussian packet the product Δx·Δp equals ħ/2 exactly.
The AI receives noisy product measurements at different widths.
It searches for ħ such that ħ/2 best matches every product — discovering the quantum of action from uncertainty alone.

packet.title: Position packet |ψ(x)|²
packet.desc: Localized in x — a narrow packet needs many momentum components.

particle.title: Momentum packet |φ(p)|²
particle.desc: Fourier partner of |ψ(x)|². Narrower in x ⇒ broader in p.

nuclear_reactor.title: Nuclear Reactor — How a PWR Makes Electricity
nuclear_reactor.desc: A simple model of a real Pressurised Water Reactor: fission heat → hot water → steam → turbine → electricity. Follow steps ①–⑤ in 3D.
nuclear_reactor.hint: Drag to orbit · click a part for a plain explanation · use rods & pump on the right
nuclear_reactor.note: Think of control rods as a power dial: IN = quieter, OUT = louder. The pump is the cooling fan. If you make lots of heat without enough cooling, the plant trips.

principle.desc: A nuclear power plant does not burn fuel like coal. It splits uranium atoms (fission). That heat boils water into steam, and steam turns a turbine that makes electricity — the same idea as many power stations, but the heat source is nuclear. In a PWR the water that touches the fuel stays in a closed loop and never mixes with the steam that spins the turbine.
principle.equation: Heat from fission  →  steam  →  spinning turbine  →  electricity
principle.observe: In 3D follow the orange labels ①→⑤. Pull rods OUT to raise power; push IN to shut down. Raise pump flow to keep the core cool. Try to match the yellow demand line in 2D.

guide.title: Energy path (read this first)
guide.s2: Pump moves hot water to the steam generator.
guide.s3: Steam generator: heat boils clean water into steam.
guide.s4: Steam spins the turbine → generator → electricity.
guide.s5: Condenser cools steam back to water; loop repeats.
guide.tip: Click any machine for a longer tip. Orange pipes = hot water · blue = cooled water · white = steam.

how.title: What should I do?
how.body: Your job is to run the plant safely and make about as much electricity as the grid asks for.
how.a: Start: rods ~30–40% in, pump ~70%. Watch the status label.
how.b: Need more power? Slowly pull rods OUT (slider down toward 0%).
how.c: Core getting hot? Raise the pump, or push rods back IN.
how.d: Trip / red warning? Push rods fully IN and raise flow, then try again.

controls.title: Your controls
controls.rodsHelp: 0% = rods pulled out → strongest fission. 100% = rods fully in → reactor almost off. Move slowly.
controls.flowHelp: How hard the pump pushes water through the core. Low pump + high power = overheating.
controls.demand: How much electricity the city wants
controls.demandHelp: Target for the generator. In 2D, match the green power line to this yellow demand.

status.shutdown: Off — control rods are fully in
status.trip: TRIP — too hot; push rods in!

ai.title: AI — How strongly do rods cut power?
ai.desc: Collect plant readings at many rod positions. The AI finds how steeply power falls when rods go in.
ai.how:
Pushing rods in does not cut power in a straight line.
The AI gets noisy power readings at many rod settings.
It searches for α in P ∝ (1 − rod)^α — a simple model of “how strong the rods are.”

core.title: ① Nuclear fuel (core)
core.desc: Uranium fuel rods. Atom splitting releases heat. Brighter = more heat. This is step ① of the plant.

rods.title: Control rods — your power dial
rods.desc: They absorb neutrons. In = quieter reactor. Out = louder. Move them slowly, like a real operator.

vessel.title: ① Pressure vessel
vessel.desc: Thick steel pot around the core. High pressure keeps water liquid even when very hot (PWR).

sg.title: ③ Steam generator
sg.desc: Hot primary water heats clean secondary water into steam. The two waters never mix — important for safety.

turbine.title: ④ Turbine hall
turbine.desc: Steam hits blades and spins a shaft. Same idea as a windmill, but driven by steam.

generator.title: ④ Generator
generator.desc: Converts the spinning shaft into electric power for the grid (the MW number you see).

pump.title: ② Coolant pump
pump.desc: Moves water: core → steam generator → back. Your cooling control. Too little flow risks a trip.

condenser.title: ⑤ Condenser & cooling tower
condenser.desc: Turns used steam back into water and dumps leftover heat. Then the water can be boiled again.

nuclear_fission.title: Nuclear Fission — Chain Reaction
nuclear_fission.desc: Dual 2D|3D chain-reaction lab: k gauge, generation bars, U-235 grid, fragments & neutrons. Presets for sub/critical/supercritical.
nuclear_fission.hint: 2D|3D · Fire a neutron · raise enrichment to grow the chain · lower it to die out
nuclear_fission.note: k = neutrons next generation / neutrons now. More U-235 → higher k. k<1 dies out, k≈1 steady, k>1 grows. (Reactor rods are a separate lab.)

principle.desc: A slow neutron can split a uranium-235 nucleus into two lighter fragments, free 2–3 more neutrons, and release about 200 MeV. If those neutrons cause more fissions, you get a chain reaction. This lab shows that general process — not reactor control hardware.
principle.equation: U-235 + n → fragments A + B + (2–3)n + ~200 MeV    ·    k = N_next / N_now
principle.observe: Orange = U-235 (can fission). Grey = U-238 (usually absorbs/scatters). Blue = neutron. Orange pieces flying out = fission fragments.

guide.title: What you are watching
guide.s1: Blue neutron flies into the uranium grid.
guide.s2: If it hits orange U-235 → FISSION (flash + two fragments).
guide.s3: New neutrons fly out — they may hit more U-235.
guide.s4: Higher enrichment (more U-235) → chain more likely to grow.
guide.tip: Press "Fire neutron". Try low enrichment (dies out) then high enrichment (grows).

how.title: How to use this lab
how.a: Fire a neutron and watch one fission (flash + fragments + new neutrons).
how.b: Raise enrichment — more orange U-235 → chain continues more easily.
how.c: Lower enrichment — mostly grey U-238 → chain dies out.
how.d: Switch to 3D to see the same grid in space.

controls.title: Controls
controls.enrichmentHelp: Percent of nuclei that are fissile U-235 (rest mostly U-238).

ai.title: AI — Finds critical enrichment
ai.desc: Collect (enrichment → k) data. AI finds enrichment that makes k≈1.
ai.how:
Criticality needs k≈1.
The AI sees noisy k at many enrichments and searches for the % that best gives k=1.

fuel.title: Uranium nuclei
fuel.desc: Orange U-235 can fission; grey U-238 usually does not.

nuclear_fusion.title: Nuclear Fusion — D–T Reaction
nuclear_fusion.desc: Dual 2D|3D D–T fusion: tokamak plasma view, 4 collision lanes, Coulomb barrier plot, cumulative energy. Ignite preset for demo.
nuclear_fusion.hint: 2D|3D · raise T toward 400–600 MK for frequent fusion · watch barrier vs KE
nuclear_fusion.note: Positive nuclei repel (Coulomb barrier). High T gives kinetic energy so they can get close enough for the strong force to fuse them.

principle.desc: Fusion joins light nuclei. Deuterium + tritium make helium-4, a neutron, and 17.6 MeV. On Earth we need huge temperatures because both nuclei are positively charged and repel until they get extremely close.
principle.observe: Top: D and T approach. Red dashed line = repulsion. Flash = fusion (He + n). Bottom plot: red barrier vs green KE from temperature.

guide.title: What you are watching
guide.s1: D (blue) and T (purple) fly toward each other.
guide.s2: Positive charges push them apart (Coulomb barrier).
guide.s3: If hot enough, they fuse → He + neutron + 17.6 MeV.
guide.s4: If too cold, they bounce — raise T and try again.
guide.tip: Watch the green KE line climb toward the red barrier as you heat the plasma.

how.title: How to use this lab
how.body: Fusion needs heat to beat electrical repulsion.
how.a: Keep T low — you should see bounce / repel.
how.b: Raise temperature until fusion flashes appear often.
how.c: Increase confinement — particles stay together longer → higher fuse chance.
how.d: Compare 2D barrier plot with 3D tokamak ring collision.

controls.title: Plasma controls
controls.tempHelp: Higher T (up to 600 MK) → faster nuclei → frequent fusion. At low T they bounce.
controls.confinementHelp: How well we keep particles together (tokamak-style boost).

ai.title: AI — Finds ignition temperature
ai.desc: Collect (T → fusion probability). AI finds T where P≈50%.
ai.how:
Fusion probability rises with temperature.
The AI fits noisy P(T) to find where P crosses about one half.

radioactive_decay.title: Radioactive Decay Simulator
radioactive_decay.desc: Choose an isotope (C-14…), set N₀ up to 10,000, and watch probabilistic decay — green bars vs the ideal exponential law.
radioactive_decay.hint: Pick C-14 · N₀ = 10,000 · watch green bars fall with random noise around the blue ideal curve
radioactive_decay.note: Each nucleus decays independently at random. Half-life is the average time for half the remaining nuclei to decay. Large N still shows statistical scatter around the ideal curve.

principle.desc: Radioactivity is random for each nucleus but predictable for a large sample. The number of undecayed nuclei falls exponentially. After one half-life, about half remain; after two, about a quarter — with random statistical variation around that average.
principle.equation: N(t)=N_0 e^{-\lambda t}\quad\cdot\quad T_{1/2}=\ln 2/\lambda\quad\cdot\quad A=\lambda N
principle.observe: Try Carbon-14 with N₀ = 10,000. Green bars = this random sample; blue curve = ideal law. Markers show 1×, 2×, 3× half-life. Reset to see a new noisy path.

guide.title: What you are watching
guide.s1: Each nucleus waits a random time, then decays (probabilistic).
guide.s2: Green bars show live N(t); blue curve is the ideal exponential.
guide.s3: Noise around the blue curve is real statistical fluctuation.
guide.tip: Compare N₀ = 100 vs 10,000 — larger samples hug the ideal curve more tightly.

how.title: How to use this lab
how.body: Random each atom — predictable as a crowd.
how.b: Set initial atoms — try 10,000 — then watch the bar chart.
how.c: Compare sample N to the ideal blue curve (noise = probability).
how.d: Reset for a new random run; shorten lab T½ to speed the demo.

controls.title: Sample
controls.n0Help: Quick presets. Each nucleus is simulated with a random chance to decay each step.
controls.n0FineHelp: 100–10,000 nuclei. Above ~400, the grid shows a subsample; the count is still fully probabilistic.
controls.halfLifeHelp: Animation clock (seconds). Physical half-life is shown below — e.g. C-14 is 5,730 years.

ai.title: AI — Discovers half-life
ai.desc: Collect noisy N(t)/N₀ points. AI finds T½.
ai.how:
The shape of the decay curve encodes T½.
The AI searches for the half-life that best fits the noisy fractions.

cloud.title: Nucleus cloud
cloud.desc: Each sphere represents nuclei in the sample. Decay is random; the average wait is the half-life.

binding_energy.title: Binding Energy per Nucleon
binding_energy.desc: B/A vs mass number: one plot explains fission and fusion — climb toward iron-56, with animated highlights and energy bars.
binding_energy.hint: Toggle fission / fusion · pick ²³⁵U or ²³⁸U · watch arrows and energy released

principle.desc: The binding energy per nucleon B/A peaks near iron-56. Light nuclei can fuse upward; heavy nuclei can fission into more tightly bound fragments — both release energy.
principle.equation: B/A(A) peak ≈ 8.8 MeV at Fe · ΔE from moving up the curve
principle.observe: Red arrows: U fission splits to medium A. Green: D+T fusion moves up from light A.

alpha_beta_decay.title: Alpha & Beta Decay Schemes
alpha_beta_decay.desc: Nucleon diagrams, energy-level schemes, and spectra for α, β⁻, β⁺, and γ — including Co-60 cascade and PET β⁺.
alpha_beta_decay.hint: Pick a scheme · watch decays animate · compare continuous β vs discrete α/γ lines

principle.desc: Alpha decay ejects ⁴He (ΔZ=−2). Beta decay converts n→p (β⁻, ΔZ=+1) or p→n (β⁺, ΔZ=−1). Gamma de-excites daughter levels with discrete photon energies. Beta spectra are continuous because the neutrino carries variable energy.
principle.observe: Left: proton (red) / neutron (gray) before & after. Centre: level diagram with transition arrows. Bottom: spectrum shape for each radiation type.

nai_spectrometer.title: NaI(Tl) Gamma Spectrometer
nai_spectrometer.desc: Scintillation MCA spectrum: photopeak, Compton continuum & edge, backscatter, and energy resolution (FWHM).
nai_spectrometer.hint: Watch the spectrum build · switch sources · change % resolution · toggle feature labels

principle.desc: A γ ray deposits energy in NaI(Tl). Scintillation light reaches a PMT; pulse height is proportional to deposited energy. Full absorption → photopeak. Partial Compton scatter → continuum up to the Compton edge. Finite light/statistics broaden peaks (FWHM).
principle.observe: Green = photopeak · orange band = Compton continuum · pink = backscatter. Widen resolution % to smear peaks.

controls.title: Spectrometer
controls.resolutionHelp: Typical NaI ≈ 6–8% FWHM at 662 keV. Higher % = broader peaks.

features.title: Spectrum features
features.photopeakBody: Full γ energy absorbed (photoelectric + multi-scatters that sum). Marks the true line energy.
features.comptonBody: γ scatters once and escapes; only the recoil electron’s energy is recorded — a broad distribution.
features.edgeBody: Maximum energy transferable in a single scatter (180°). Continuum ends near E_C.
features.backscatterBody: γ scatters ~180° in surrounding material, then enters the crystal at reduced energy.
features.resolutionBody: Peak width FWHM from light statistics & noise. R = FWHM/E; improves roughly as 1/√E.

gm_dead_time.title: GM Tube: Energy Response & Dead Time
gm_dead_time.desc: Why a Geiger counter cannot measure energy, how dead time loses counts at high rate, and the HV plateau.
gm_dead_time.hint: Switch views · raise true rate · widen τ · sweep HV across the plateau

principle.desc: In the Geiger region the avalanche saturates, so pulse height is independent of deposited energy — you get counts, not a spectrum. After each count the tube is “dead” for time τ; at high true rates m many events are missed. Non-paralyzable model: n = m/(1+mτ).
principle.observe: Green pulses = counted · red = lost in τ. Gold dot = your (m,n) on the curve. Energy view: flat bars vs proportional rising bars.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.dead1: Dead time τ: tube recovering after a pulse; events in that window are not counted.
teach.dead2: Non-paralyzable formula n = m/(1+mτ). At mτ ≪ 1 losses are small; at mτ ~ 1 half the events are lost.
teach.dead3: Correct true rate from observed: m = n/(1−nτ) — only if nτ < 1.
teach.en1: Geiger pulses saturate → same height for 59 keV or 1332 keV.
teach.en2: A proportional counter’s pulse height grows with energy — basis of spectroscopy.
teach.en3: For energy spectra use NaI, HPGe, or Si — not a plain GM tube.
teach.pl1: Count rate rises with HV, then flattens on the Geiger plateau — the working region.
teach.pl2: Too low HV: incomplete avalanches / low efficiency. Too high: continuous discharge.
teach.pl3: Pick a voltage mid-plateau so small HV drift barely changes the count rate.

geiger_counter.title: Geiger Counter & Sources
geiger_counter.desc: Count rate vs distance (inverse square) and lead shielding — Poisson ticks on a teaching GM tube model.
geiger_counter.hint: 2D|3D · move source · add lead mm · watch count histogram

principle.desc: Geiger–Müller tubes detect ionizing radiation as discrete clicks. Count rate drops with distance (~1/r² geometry) and falls exponentially through absorber (μ·x).
principle.observe: Cyan rings = flux spread. Shield slab between source and tube cuts rate.

hpge_vs_nai.title: HPGe vs NaI Resolution
hpge_vs_nai.desc: Overlay MCA spectra for the same γ source — sharp HPGe peaks (~0.2%) vs broad NaI (~7%), FWHM and R = FWHM/E.
hpge_vs_nai.hint: Pick Cs-137 or Co-60 · slide both resolutions · watch peaks separate or smear

principle.desc: Energy resolution R = FWHM/E. NaI(Tl) scintillators (~6–8% at 662 keV) are cheap and room-temperature. High-purity germanium (~0.2%) resolves close lines but needs cryogenic cooling to keep leakage noise low.
principle.observe: Cyan = NaI spectrum · green = HPGe. Co-60: HPGe shows two clean peaks; NaI may blend them.

controls.title: Compare detectors
controls.naiResHelp: Typical NaI ≈ 6–8% FWHM. Higher % = broader peaks.

features.title: Why it matters
features.resolutionBody: R = FWHM/E. At 662 keV, ~7% NaI vs ~0.2% HPGe — order-of-magnitude sharper semiconductor peaks.
features.coolingBody: Cryogenic LN₂ or electromechanical coolers suppress leakage current so electronic noise does not wipe out the resolution advantage.
features.costBody: NaI is cheaper, larger volumes are practical, and it runs at room temperature — great for surveys and teaching labs.
features.useBody: Use HPGe for nuclide ID and close lines; use NaI for efficiency, cost, and rugged field work.

alpha_spectroscopy.title: Si Detector α Spectroscopy
alpha_spectroscopy.desc: Discrete α lines (Am-241, Pu-239, …) with excellent vacuum resolution; air path shifts and smears peaks.
alpha_spectroscopy.hint: Toggle vacuum vs air · thicken air path · watch peaks broaden and shift down

principle.desc: Silicon charged-particle detectors measure α energies with excellent resolution in vacuum. In air, α particles lose energy (dE/dx) and straggle — peaks shift to lower energy and broaden. Always run α spectroscopy in vacuum (or with a tiny source–detector gap).
principle.observe: Green dashed = vacuum line energies. With air, gold spectrum shifts left and widens.

controls.title: α chamber
controls.airHelp: More air → more energy loss and straggling (teaching model).

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: α lines are discrete MeV energies — Am-241 ≈ 5.486 MeV is a common calibration line.
teach.t2: Vacuum is essential: even a few mm of air shifts and smears peaks.
teach.t3: Si detectors give excellent α resolution (~tens of keV) when the path is clean.
teach.t4: Close multiplets (Pu-239) need vacuum + good resolution to separate.

neutron_detector.title: ³He & BF₃ Proportional Counters
neutron_detector.desc: Detect neutrons via capture charged products; thermal ≫ fast efficiency; optional moderator and wall effect.
neutron_detector.hint: Switch ³He ↔ BF₃ · sweep neutron energy · toggle moderator / wall effect

principle.desc: Neutrons are neutral and leave little direct ionization. Gas proportional counters detect them through capture reactions that yield charged particles: ³He(n,p)³H or ¹⁰B(n,α)⁷Li. Thermal neutrons are detected far more efficiently than fast ones; a moderator helps thermalize a fast beam.
principle.observe: Efficiency curve peaks at thermal. Pulse-height peak near Q; continuum = wall effect.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Principle: neutrons → capture → charged products → ionization pulse.
teach.t2: Thermal efficiency ≫ fast; use a moderator when the beam is fast.
teach.t3: ³He generally offers higher thermal sensitivity than BF₃ at similar fill (teaching model).
teach.t4: Wall effect and dead time can distort pulse-height spectra at high rate — note them in real labs.

pet_coincidence.title: PET 511 keV Coincidence
pet_coincidence.desc: β⁺ annihilation → two back-to-back 511 keV γ; true vs scatter vs random coincidences; link to FDG imaging.
pet_coincidence.hint: Raise activity · widen coincidence window · watch randoms grow

principle.desc: A positron annihilates with an electron producing two 511 keV photons ~180° apart. PET accepts events when both detectors fire within a coincidence window. True coincidences map the line of response; scatter and randoms add noise. FDG (¹⁸F) is a common metabolic tracer.
principle.observe: Green flash = true pair. Bars: true / scatter / random rates vs activity and window.

controls.title: PET lab
controls.activityHelp: Higher activity raises trues and (faster) randoms.
controls.geometryHelp: Teaching stand-in for solid-angle / ring coverage.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Annihilation → two 511 keV γ back-to-back; coincidence defines a line of response (LOR).
teach.t2: True: both photons from the same annihilation, unscattered.
teach.t3: Scatter: one (or both) Compton-scattered — wrong LOR. Random: unrelated singles within τ.
teach.t4: Medicine: FDG-PET maps glucose uptake; timing window and activity affect image noise.

wheatstone_bridge.title: Wheatstone Bridge Resistance Measurement
wheatstone_bridge.desc: Balance a four-arm resistor bridge (R1, R2, R3, Rx) with a galvanometer null to measure an unknown resistance precisely.
wheatstone_bridge.hint: 1) Treat R1,R2,R3 as known · 2) Adjust Rx until the galvanometer centers · 3) Read Rx = R2·R3/R1

principle.desc: A Wheatstone bridge is two voltage dividers sharing one battery. Left divider: R1 over R3. Right divider: R2 over Rx. A galvanometer connects the midpoints. When both midpoints are at the same voltage, no current flows through the galvanometer — the bridge is balanced. That null condition is R1·Rx = R2·R3, so the unknown is Rx = R2·R3/R1. Because you only look for zero current, battery drift and galvanometer scale errors cancel out — that is why bridges are precise.
principle.equation: R_1 R_x = R_2 R_3 \quad\Rightarrow\quad R_x = \dfrac{R_2 R_3}{R_1};;V_g \approx V\left(\frac{R_3}{R_1+R_3} - \frac{R_x}{R_2+R_x}\right)
principle.observe: Needle centers + green = balanced. Lower plot: Vg vs Rx crosses zero at the balance point.

controls.title: Bridge controls
controls.R1Help: Known reference resistor in the top-left arm.
controls.R2Help: Known reference resistor in the top-right arm.
controls.R3Help: Known, adjustable resistor used to null the bridge.
controls.RxHelp: The unknown resistance you are trying to measure — find the balance point.
controls.VHelp: Supply voltage across the top-bottom diagonal. At true balance, V does not change the null.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Balance condition: R1·Rx = R2·R3, so Rx = R2·R3/R1 — a ratio of known resistors, not an absolute measurement.
teach.t2: At balance the galvanometer carries zero current: both middle nodes sit at the same potential.
teach.t3: Because balance is a null condition, the result is insensitive to battery voltage drift or galvanometer calibration — this is what makes bridge methods self-calibrating and precise.
teach.t4: Off balance, the small bridge voltage Vg ≈ V·[R3/(R1+R3) − Rx/(R2+Rx)] tells you which way to adjust the arms to reach balance.

thermionic_emission.title: Thermionic Emission
thermionic_emission.desc: Heated cathode emits electrons over the work function; Richardson-Dushman J = A T² e^(−W/kT), vacuum-diode temperature-limited vs space-charge-limited I-V curve.
thermionic_emission.hint: 1) Heat the cathode · 2) Sweep anode V · 3) Spot when the diode switches from Child–Langmuir to Richardson saturation

principle.desc: Electrons in a metal sit behind a work-function barrier W. Heat the cathode and the high-energy tail of the thermal distribution can escape — thermionic emission. The maximum emission density is the Richardson–Dushman law J = A T² exp(−W/k_B T). In a vacuum diode the real current is limited by whichever is smaller: that Richardson saturation (temperature-limited), or Child–Langmuir space-charge current (I ∝ V^{3/2}) when many electrons already fill the gap at low anode voltage.
principle.equation: J = A T^2 e^{-W/(k_B T)};;I_{\mathrm{CL}} \propto V^{3/2}\quad(\text{space-charge limited})
principle.observe: Gold dot = operating point on the I–V curve. Filament brightens with T; electron dots race to the anode.

controls.title: Vacuum diode lab
controls.THelp: Hotter cathode → far more electrons cross the work function barrier (exponential dependence).
controls.WHelp: Lower work function → easier emission at the same temperature.
controls.VHelp: Low V: space-charge-limited (Child-Langmuir). High V: temperature-limited (Richardson saturation).

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Thermal energy lets some conduction electrons overcome the work function W and leave the hot cathode surface.
teach.t2: J = A T² e^(−W/k_BT): emission is exponentially sensitive to temperature and to work function.
teach.t3: At low anode voltage the diode is space-charge-limited (I ∝ V^1.5); at high voltage it saturates at the Richardson current — temperature-limited.
teach.t4: This is the Edison effect: the working principle behind vacuum-tube diodes, CRTs, and electron guns.

photomultiplier_tube.title: Photomultiplier Tube
photomultiplier_tube.desc: Photons eject photoelectrons at a photocathode; a dynode cascade multiplies the electron cloud stage by stage into a huge anode current — G = δⁿ.
photomultiplier_tube.hint: 1) Set light + QE · 2) Raise dynode voltage (δ) · 3) Add stages n · watch gain explode as δⁿ

principle.desc: A photon hitting the photocathode can eject a photoelectron (photoelectric effect). That electron is accelerated into the first dynode and knocks out several secondary electrons (yield δ, which rises with inter-dynode voltage). Each dynode repeats the multiplication. After n stages the gain is G = δⁿ, so a single photon can become a large anode pulse — I_out = I_cathode · G.
principle.observe: Photon → cathode → multiplying cloud at each dynode → bright anode burst. Red plot marker = G(n).

controls.title: PMT lab
controls.intensityHelp: More incident photons means a larger photocathode current.
controls.qeHelp: Fraction of incident photons that eject a photoelectron.
controls.voltageHelp: Higher voltage accelerates electrons harder, raising the secondary emission yield δ.
controls.nStagesHelp: Gain compounds as G = δⁿ (scene shows a representative cascade).

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Photoelectric effect: photons striking the photocathode eject photoelectrons — current ∝ light intensity × quantum efficiency.
teach.t2: Each dynode impact releases δ secondary electrons, multiplying the cloud stage by stage through the chain.
teach.t3: After n dynodes the total gain is G = δⁿ, growing exponentially — a few extra stages can add orders of magnitude.
teach.t4: The huge amplification I_out = I_cathode · G lets a PMT turn a single absorbed photon into a measurable current pulse.

glow_discharge.title: Glow Discharge Tube
glow_discharge.desc: Low-pressure DC gas tube: below Paschen breakdown voltage no current flows; above it, a self-maintained glow with cathode glow, negative glow, and positive column bands.
glow_discharge.hint: 1) Read V_b from p·d on the Paschen curve · 2) Raise V above V_b · 3) Watch cathode glow / negative glow / positive column

principle.desc: Free electrons accelerate, ionize gas atoms, and start an avalanche. Ions hitting the cathode free more electrons (γ). When that feedback sustains the avalanche, the gas breaks down — a self-maintained glow. Paschen’s law says the breakdown voltage V_b depends only on the product p·d (pressure × gap). The Paschen curve is U-shaped: both very small and very large p·d need higher voltage to strike.
principle.observe: Colored point = (p·d, V_b). Dashed line = applied V. Tube lights in bands only when V > V_b.

controls.title: Discharge tube
controls.pressureHelp: Lower pressure means fewer collisions per unit length.
controls.voltageHelp: Raise V above V_b to strike and sustain the glow.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Paschen's law: breakdown voltage V_b depends only on the product p·d, not on p or d separately.
teach.t2: The Paschen curve is U-shaped — both very low and very high p·d raise V_b; a minimum lies between them.
teach.t3: Above V_b, the tube glows in bands: bright cathode glow, dark spaces, a broad negative glow, and a long positive column reaching the anode.
teach.t4: This is the same physics behind neon signs and fluorescent tubes — different zones of ionization, recombination, and excitation along the current path.

arc_discharge.title: Electric Arc Discharge
arc_discharge.desc: High-current, low-voltage, thermally-sustained arc between two electrodes: negative differential resistance, live falling V–I characteristic.
arc_discharge.hint: 1) Raise current I · 2) Watch V fall (dV/dI < 0) · 3) Widen gap L and see the whole curve shift up

principle.desc: An electric arc is a hot, thermally sustained discharge. A tiny cathode spot is so hot it emits electrons thermionically, so the arc carries huge current at relatively low voltage — unlike a cold-cathode glow. Empirically the V–I curve falls: raising I lowers V (negative differential resistance), often written with Ayrton’s form. Power P = VI is still large because I is large. In a real circuit you need a ballast so current cannot run away.
principle.observe: Gold dot = operating point on the falling V–I curve. Channel brightens/thickens as I rises.

controls.title: Arc lab
controls.IHelp: Raise I and watch arc voltage V fall — negative differential resistance.
controls.LHelp: Increase the electrode gap to see the V–I curve shift to higher voltage.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: An arc's thermionic cathode spot supplies electrons freely, so current is high while voltage stays comparatively low.
teach.t2: Negative differential resistance: dV/dI < 0 — raising current LOWERS arc voltage, opposite to an ordinary resistor.
teach.t3: Arc power P = VI is very high despite modest V, because I is large — this is why arcs weld, melt, and light intensely.
teach.t4: Because dV/dI < 0, an arc needs a ballast (series resistor, reactor, or current-limited supply) to prevent current runaway.

spark_discharge.title: Spark Discharge
spark_discharge.desc: Transient gas-gap breakdown at the Paschen voltage V_b(p·d); RC relaxation oscillator charges a capacitor toward V_supply and sparks over each time it reaches V_b, producing a repeating sawtooth.
spark_discharge.hint: 1) Set p,d → V_b · 2) Ensure V_supply > V_b · 3) Tune R,C and watch sawtooth spark rate

principle.desc: A spark is a brief, self-extinguishing breakdown of a gas gap when voltage reaches the Paschen threshold V_b(p·d). The classic lab circuit is an RC relaxation oscillator: capacitor C charges through R from V_supply. When V_C hits V_b the gap fires, dumps the capacitor, and charging starts again — a sawtooth on the scope and a flash each cycle. If V_supply < V_b, the gap never sparks.
principle.observe: Scope sawtooth climbs; white/blue flash at each reset. Info panel shows charge time and spark frequency.

controls.title: Spark gap lab
controls.pressureHelp: Gas pressure between the electrodes — changes p·d and thus V_b.
controls.spacingHelp: Electrode separation — changes p·d and thus V_b.
controls.VsupplyHelp: Must exceed V_b for the gap to ever spark.
controls.RHelp: Larger R slows capacitor charging — fewer sparks per second.
controls.CHelp: Larger C slows capacitor charging — fewer sparks per second.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: A spark is a transient breakdown — it self-extinguishes once the capacitor discharges, unlike a self-sustained glow or arc discharge.
teach.t2: Paschen's law sets the breakdown voltage V_b(p·d); pressure and gap spacing both shift p·d along the U-shaped curve.
teach.t3: The RC charging time to reach V_b sets the spark period; increasing R or C makes sparks less frequent.
teach.t4: If V_supply never exceeds V_b, the capacitor asymptotically approaches V_supply and the gap never fires.

corona_discharge.title: Corona Discharge
corona_discharge.desc: Localized self-sustained ionization at a sharp point or thin wire once the local field exceeds Peek's-law threshold — even when the average gap field stays low.
corona_discharge.hint: 1) Sharpen the tip (small r) · 2) Raise V · 3) Watch a violet halo at the tip only when E_tip > E_onset

principle.desc: Charge crowds onto a sharp conductor, so the local field at a needle tip can be huge even when the average gap field is modest. Peek’s law gives the onset field E_onset for air corona. When E_tip > E_onset a thin, self-sustained glow appears at the tip only — not a full spark across the gap. The same tip physics appears in lightning rods and ESP corona wires.
principle.observe: Violet-blue halo + short streamers at the needle tip only. Plot: E_tip vs Peek E_onset.

controls.title: Corona lab
controls.VHelp: Raise voltage to increase the field everywhere, including at the tip.
controls.rHelp: Smaller r = sharper point = much higher local field for the same voltage.
controls.dHelp: Distance from needle tip to the grounded plane.
controls.deltaHelp: Relative air density (1.0 = standard conditions); drops with altitude or heat, lowering the onset field.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Corona is LOCAL: it ignites only where the field is locally concentrated — at a sharp point, thin wire, or sharp edge — not across the whole gap.
teach.t2: Peek's law: E_onset = 30δ(1 + 0.301/√(δr)) kV/cm — sharper points (smaller r) have a lower onset field, so they corona at lower voltage.
teach.t3: Lower air density δ (higher altitude, higher temperature) lowers E_onset, so corona ignites more easily under those conditions.
teach.t4: Real-world corona: power-line hissing and losses, the ozone smell near high-voltage gear, St. Elmo's fire, and the deliberate point-discharge design of lightning rods and precipitators.

lightning_rod.title: Lightning Rod (Franklin Rod)
lightning_rod.desc: Sharp grounded rod: field concentration + preferred strike attachment + safe path to ground; rolling-sphere protection radius.
lightning_rod.hint: 1) Set rod height h · 2) Set design current I · 3) Read r_s and protection radius R_p from the rolling sphere

principle.desc: A lightning rod is a sharp, grounded conductor. The tip concentrates the field (mild corona can bleed some charge), but the critical job is preferential attachment: a nearby strike prefers the rod’s low-impedance path to earth instead of the building. The rolling-sphere method estimates the protected zone: a sphere of radius equal to the striking distance r_s rolled over the structure must not touch the building without first touching the rod.
principle.observe: Dashed arc = rolling sphere; shaded triangle = protected zone; gold marker = (I, R_p).

controls.title: Rod & strike
controls.hHelp: Height of the rod tip above the structure's peak.
controls.IHelp: Prospective peak current of the strike being protected against.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Two roles: field concentration at the sharp tip discourages a strike from starting at the structure, and the grounded rod gives any nearby strike a safe, low-impedance path to earth.
teach.t2: Unlike an ungrounded sharp point (corona discharge alone), the rod's connection to ground is what actually carries the strike current away safely.
teach.t3: Rolling-sphere method: a sphere of radius r_s = 10·I^0.65 rolled over the structure traces the boundary of the protected zone.
teach.t4: Taller rods and larger design currents both increase the protection radius R_p, until h ≥ r_s where the geometry saturates.

electrolysis_copper.title: Copper Sulfate Electrolysis
electrolysis_copper.desc: Electrorefining cell: Cu²⁺ deposits at the cathode, copper anode dissolves — Faraday's laws relate mass deposited to current and time.
electrolysis_copper.hint: 1) Set current I · 2) Set run time t · 3) Compare deposit growth with m = ItM/(zF)

principle.desc: In a copper sulfate cell with copper electrodes, cathode reduction plates solid copper (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu) while the anode oxidizes and dissolves (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻). Charge transferred is Q = It. Faraday’s laws: moles deposited n = Q/(zF) and mass m = nM = ItM/(zF), with z = 2 for Cu²⁺ and F Faraday’s constant. Because both electrodes are copper, bath concentration stays roughly steady — the idea behind electrorefining.
principle.equation: Q = It\quad\cdot\quad n = \dfrac{Q}{zF}\quad\cdot\quad m = \dfrac{I t M}{zF}
principle.observe: Deposit thickens on the cathode; anode thins slightly. Blue marker = elapsed time on the m–t line.

controls.title: Electrolysis cell
controls.currentHelp: Higher current deposits copper faster (mass ∝ I at fixed t).
controls.timeHelp: Target duration for the mass–time curve (not a wall-clock stopwatch).

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Faraday's law: n = It/(zF), m = nM — mass deposited is directly proportional to charge Q = It.
teach.t2: Cathode (reduction): Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu — copper plates out and the cathode gains mass.
teach.t3: Anode (oxidation): Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ — the copper anode dissolves and loses mass.
teach.t4: Because the anode is copper too, copper is transferred from anode to cathode and the CuSO₄ bath concentration stays roughly constant — the basis of electrorefining and electroplating.

pn_junction.title: Rectification of a P-N Junction
pn_junction.desc: The diode I–V curve and how a single diode (half-wave) or a four-diode bridge (full-wave) turns AC into pulsating DC.
pn_junction.hint: Switch views · sweep bias voltage or AC amplitude/frequency · toggle a smoothing capacitor

principle.desc: A p-n junction conducts easily when forward biased (p-side positive) and blocks current when reverse biased, because forward bias narrows the depletion region and lets majority carriers diffuse across, while reverse bias widens it. The Shockley equation I = Is·(e^(V/nVt) − 1) captures this asymmetry. Fed with an AC input, a diode passes only the half-cycle that forward-biases it (half-wave); four diodes in a bridge fold both half-cycles the same way (full-wave). A capacitor across the load smooths the pulses into a nearly steady DC level.
principle.observe: I-V view: gold dot is your bias point on the exponential curve. Rectifier view: grey = input AC, green = rectified output.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.j1: The depletion region is a carrier-free zone at the junction where fixed acceptor (−) and donor (+) ions are exposed, creating a built-in field.
teach.j2: Forward bias pushes holes and electrons together — they cross the narrowed junction and recombine, sustaining a real diffusion current.
teach.j3: Reverse bias pulls carriers away from the junction, widening the depletion region so only a tiny minority-carrier leakage current flows.
teach.iv1: Forward bias narrows the depletion region — current rises exponentially above the ~0.6 V knee.
teach.iv2: Reverse bias widens the depletion region — only a tiny leakage current flows.
teach.iv3: Vt = kT/q ≈ 26 mV at room temperature sets how sharply the exponential rises.
teach.r1: Half-wave: one diode conducts on the positive half-cycle only; the negative half is thrown away.
teach.r2: Full-wave bridge: four diodes route both half-cycles the same direction through the load.
teach.r3: A smoothing capacitor charges on each peak and discharges slowly through the load, cutting ripple.

seebeck_effect.title: Thermoelectric Power (Seebeck Effect)
seebeck_effect.desc: A temperature difference across a junction of two dissimilar metals generates an open-circuit EMF — the working principle of a thermocouple.
seebeck_effect.hint: Pick a metal pair · set hot- and cold-junction temperatures · watch the EMF vs ΔT curve

principle.desc: When two different conductors are joined and the junctions are held at different temperatures, free carriers diffuse from the hot junction toward the cold one at different rates in the two metals, building up a net EMF proportional to the temperature difference. The proportionality constant S (the Seebeck coefficient of the pair) is tiny — tens of microvolts per kelvin — which is why practical thermocouples use long wires and precise cold-junction references.
principle.observe: Hot junction (left) glows warm, cold junction (right) glows cool. Yellow dots drift along the loop at a rate set by the EMF.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: V = S·(Th − Tc): EMF grows linearly with the temperature difference, not the absolute temperature.
teach.t2: S depends on the pair of materials, not on wire length or thickness — that's why thermocouples are named by their metal pair (K, J, T type…).
teach.t3: Real thermocouple circuits need a known cold-junction reference, since only the difference between the two junctions is measured.

peltier_effect.title: Inverse Thermoelectric Effect (Peltier)
peltier_effect.desc: Driving a current through a junction of two dissimilar conductors pumps heat from one side to the other — the Seebeck effect run backwards, used in thermoelectric coolers.
peltier_effect.hint: Sweep the current (sign reverses hot/cold sides) · watch the cold-face ΔT settle to equilibrium

principle.desc: The Peltier effect is the reverse of the Seebeck effect: forcing a current I through a junction of two dissimilar conductors makes one side absorb heat and the other release it, because carriers carry different amounts of heat per charge in each material. The Peltier coefficient is linked to the Seebeck coefficient by the Kelvin relation Π = S·T. In a real thermoelectric cooler, Joule heating (∝ I²) and thermal conduction back-leak (∝ ΔT) both work against the useful Peltier cooling, so there is an optimum current and a maximum ΔT the device can reach.
principle.equation: \Pi = S\,T\quad\cdot\quad Q_c = \Pi I - \tfrac{1}{2}I^2 R - K\Delta T
principle.observe: Reversing the current sign swaps which face is cold. The lower chart shows the cold-face ΔT relaxing toward its equilibrium value.

controls.title: Peltier module
controls.currentHelp: Positive cools the top ceramic plate; negative reverses the polarity and heats it instead.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Π = S·T links the Peltier and Seebeck coefficients — the same junction, run in reverse.
teach.t2: Useful cooling Qc = ΠI competes with Joule heating (∝ I²) and thermal back-leak (∝ ΔT), so ΔT saturates at an equilibrium value.
teach.t3: Reversing the current swaps hot and cold faces instantly — this is how a solid-state TEC module can both cool and heat.
teach.t4: A real TEC module wires many alternating P/N semiconductor pillars in series (electrically) but in parallel (thermally) between two ceramic plates, using copper tabs — exactly the structure shown here.

topPlate.title: Ceramic plate (top)
topPlate.desc: Alumina plate that thermally couples the pillar array to the outside; it becomes the cold or hot face depending on current polarity.

bottomPlate.title: Ceramic plate (bottom)
bottomPlate.desc: The opposite ceramic plate — always the face opposite the one named above, so it swaps cold/hot with it.

pillar.title: P/N pillar
pillar.desc: One of the alternating P/N semiconductor legs. Under current, both leg types carry heat carriers from the cold face to the hot face, but electrons and holes drift in opposite electrical directions — that is why P and N legs must alternate for the heat flow to add up in series.

cyclotron.title: Cyclotron: Resonant Acceleration
cyclotron.desc: A charged particle in a uniform magnetic field orbits at a frequency independent of its speed, so a fixed-frequency dee voltage stays in resonance while the orbit spirals outward and gains energy.
cyclotron.hint: Pick a particle · set B · tune the RF/cyclotron frequency ratio near 1.00 for resonance

principle.desc: In a uniform magnetic field B, a charged particle of mass m and charge q moves on a circle whose angular frequency f = qB/2πm does not depend on its speed — faster particles simply orbit on a larger radius. A cyclotron exploits this: an oscillating voltage across the gap between two D-shaped electrodes (dees) accelerates the particle every half-turn, as long as the RF frequency matches f. Because f is speed-independent, the same RF frequency keeps working as the orbit spirals outward — until relativistic mass increase detunes it at high energy, which is why real accelerators need synchrocyclotrons or synchrotrons beyond a few tens of MeV.
principle.observe: At ratio = 1.00 the spiral grows steadily outward. Detune the ratio away from 1.00 and the kicks fall out of phase — growth stalls or reverses.

controls.title: Cyclotron lab
controls.ratioHelp: 1.00 = perfect resonance. Move away from 1.00 to see the beam fall out of phase.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: f = qB/2πm is independent of the particle's speed — this is what makes fixed-frequency acceleration possible.
teach.t2: Each gap crossing gives (or takes) a kick of energy depending on how well the RF phase matches the orbit — this is resonance.
teach.t3: Larger radius ↔ higher energy (E ∝ r²): the particle is extracted once it reaches the edge of the dees.

oscilloscope_crt.title: Electron-Beam Oscilloscope Principles
oscilloscope_crt.desc: How a cathode-ray tube traces voltage vs time using a sawtooth sweep, and how two AC signals on X and Y plates draw a Lissajous figure.
oscilloscope_crt.hint: Switch views · pick a signal shape · adjust sweep and frequency · in X-Y mode watch the ratio of fx:fy

principle.desc: In a CRT oscilloscope, an electron gun fires a narrow beam at a phosphor screen. Two pairs of deflection plates steer it: normally the horizontal plates are driven by an internal sawtooth 'time base' that sweeps the spot left to right at a constant rate, while the vertical plates carry the input signal — so the glowing trace is literally a plot of voltage vs time. If the sweep is disabled and both plate pairs are driven by their own AC signals instead (X-Y mode), the beam traces the phase relationship between the two signals, producing a Lissajous figure whose shape reveals the frequency ratio.
principle.equation: x(t) \propto \text{sweep}(t)\ ,\ y(t) \propto V_{in}(t)\quad\text{or}\quad x=A\sin(2\pi f_x t),\ y=B\sin(2\pi f_y t+\varphi)
principle.observe: Sweep view: green trace is Vy(t) against the sawtooth time base. X-Y view: closed loops mean fx:fy is a simple ratio; a drifting pattern means it isn't.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.s1: The horizontal sweep is a sawtooth: it moves the spot at a constant rate, then snaps back — this is what turns time into horizontal position.
teach.s2: The vertical plates deflect the beam proportional to the input voltage, so the glowing trace is literally y = V(t).
teach.s3: If the input completes a whole number of cycles per sweep, the trace looks stable; otherwise it appears to drift sideways.
teach.s4: Sine, square, triangle, sawtooth and pulse are all just V(t). The vertical plates copy that shape onto the screen.
teach.l1: With the sweep off, driving both axes with sine waves plots one signal against the other directly.
teach.l2: A simple integer ratio fy:fx (1:1, 2:1, 3:2…) produces a stable closed Lissajous figure.
teach.l3: The phase offset between the two signals changes the shape of the loop — 0° and 180° collapse to a line, 90° gives a circle/ellipse.

gun.title: Electron gun
gun.desc: A heated cathode boils off electrons; the grid controls how many reach the screen, and the anode ring accelerates them down the tube.

yplates.title: Vertical (Y) plates
yplates.desc: These deflect the beam up or down in proportion to the input voltage — this is what turns Vy(t) into vertical position on the screen.

xplates.title: Horizontal (X) plates
xplates.desc: These deflect the beam left or right — driven by the internal sawtooth time base in sweep mode, or by a second signal in X-Y mode.

screen.title: Phosphor screen
screen.desc: Where the beam lands, the phosphor coating glows and fades over a fraction of a second — that brief persistence is what lets a moving spot look like a continuous trace.

electron_microscope.title: Principles of the Electron Microscope
electron_microscope.desc: Accelerated electrons have a de Broglie wavelength thousands of times shorter than visible light, so magnetic 'lenses' can resolve far finer detail than any optical microscope.
electron_microscope.hint: Raise the accelerating voltage to shrink the electron wavelength · compare resolving power with light

principle.desc: Every particle has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p. Accelerating an electron through a voltage V gives it momentum p = √(2meV), so λ shrinks as V rises — at 20 kV it is roughly 100,000 times shorter than green light. Since the diffraction-limited resolution of any imaging system is d ≈ 0.61λ/NA (the Rayleigh criterion), swapping light for electrons and glass lenses for magnetic 'lenses' (coils that focus the electron beam) lets a microscope resolve individual atoms rather than being capped at roughly half the wavelength of light.
principle.observe: Left column: optical microscope with glass lenses and light. Right column: electron microscope with magnetic lenses and an electron beam. Bottom bar compares the two wavelengths on a log scale.

controls.title: Electron optics
controls.voltageHelp: Higher voltage → shorter electron wavelength → finer resolution.
controls.naHelp: Electron-lens apertures are much smaller than optical ones, which limits how much the tiny wavelength can be exploited.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: λ = h/p: faster (more energetic) electrons have shorter wavelengths, just like any other particle.
teach.t2: Resolution is diffraction-limited by wavelength, not by lens quality — this is why electrons beat light by orders of magnitude.
teach.t3: Electron-lens numerical apertures are tiny (thousandths, not ~1 like a glass lens), so the huge wavelength advantage isn't fully realized — real TEMs resolve ~0.1 nm, not picometres.

hall_effect.title: Hall Effect
hall_effect.desc: A current-carrying slab in a perpendicular magnetic field develops a sideways voltage as the Lorentz force deflects carriers to one edge — its sign reveals whether the carriers are electrons or holes.
hall_effect.hint: Choose n-type or p-type · sweep current and field · watch which edge charges up

principle.desc: Charge carriers drifting through a conductor in a magnetic field feel a sideways Lorentz force F = qv×B, which pushes them toward one edge of the sample until the resulting transverse electric field balances the magnetic force. The steady-state transverse voltage is the Hall voltage. Crucially, electrons (negative, drifting opposite to conventional current) and holes (positive, drifting with conventional current) are pushed to the same physical edge by the same current and field only if they have opposite charge sign — so the sign of the measured Hall voltage tells you directly whether a semiconductor is n-type or p-type.
principle.observe: Dots are drifting charge carriers; they pile up toward one edge. The +/− labels on the top and bottom edges flip when you switch carrier type.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: V_H = IB/(net): Hall voltage grows with current and field, and shrinks in thicker or more heavily doped samples.
teach.t2: The sign of V_H tells you the carrier type directly — this is the standard way to identify n-type vs p-type semiconductors.
teach.t3: Measuring V_H, I, B and t lets you extract the carrier density n — the basis of Hall-effect sensors and probes.

diamagnetism.title: Diamagnetic Effect
diamagnetism.desc: Every material develops a tiny induced magnetic moment that opposes an applied field; in diamagnetic materials this is the dominant response, producing a weak repulsion from strong-field regions.
diamagnetism.hint: Pick a material · sweep field and field gradient · watch it drift toward weaker or stronger field

principle.desc: An applied magnetic field induces small atomic-scale currents that, by Lenz's law, create a magnetic moment opposing the field — this is diamagnetism, and it is present in all matter. In most materials it is masked by a stronger paramagnetic or ferromagnetic response from unpaired electron spins, but in materials with no net atomic magnetic moment (bismuth, graphite, water, most organic matter) diamagnetism dominates and χ (magnetic susceptibility) is small and negative. In a field gradient this produces a real, measurable force pushing the sample toward weaker field — strong enough, with a powerful enough magnet, to levitate water or a live frog.
principle.observe: The induced-moment arrow (blue) opposes the field for diamagnetic samples. The green arrow shows the resulting force direction and strength.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: χ < 0 means the induced moment opposes the field — diamagnetism is universal but usually tiny and easily masked.
teach.t2: A field gradient (not just a strong field) is required for a net force — a perfectly uniform field exerts no force on a magnetic dipole.
teach.t3: Superconductors are the extreme case: perfect diamagnets (χ = −1) that expel field entirely — the Meissner effect.

laser_printer.title: Laser Printer Operating Principle
laser_printer.desc: Xerographic process: charge the drum, laser-discharge pixels to write a latent image, develop with toner, transfer to paper, fuse with heat and pressure.
laser_printer.hint: 1) Set charge & residual V (contrast) · 2) Set image density · 3) Keep fuser in 180–220 °C · watch the five stations

principle.desc: Laser printers use xerography on a photoconductive drum. (1) Charge: a corona (or charge roller) gives the drum a uniform surface voltage. (2) Expose: a laser discharges only the pixels of the image, leaving a residual voltage — contrast ΔV = V_charge − V_residual. (3) Develop: charged toner sticks to the discharged latent image. (4) Transfer: another field pulls toner onto paper. (5) Fuse: heat + pressure permanently bond toner (~180–220 °C). Outside that window the print smears or flakes.
principle.observe: Laser raster on the drum; toner on the discharged arc; paper strip picks up the image; fuser green = bond OK.

controls.title: Printer controls
controls.chargeVHelp: Corona wire charges the drum's surface to this magnitude before exposure.
controls.expResidualVHelp: Potential left on a pixel after the laser discharges it — lower means stronger contrast.
controls.densityHelp: Fraction of the raster line the laser exposes — higher means a darker page.
controls.fuserTempCHelp: Rollers must sit roughly in 180-220 °C to permanently bond toner to paper.

info.fuserBad: Bad bond — too hot or too cold

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: The process is strictly ordered: charge → expose → develop → transfer → fuse.
teach.t2: The laser discharges pixels — it never adds charge; toner is pulled onto the discharged, low-potential regions.
teach.t3: Contrast voltage ΔV = V_charge − V_residual sets how strongly toner sticks — bigger ΔV means darker, more saturated print.
teach.t4: Fusing needs heat and pressure in a narrow temperature window; too cold and toner flakes off, too hot and the page can smear or jam.

electrostatic_shielding.title: Electrostatic Shielding (Faraday Cage)
electrostatic_shielding.desc: Hollow conductor in an external field E₀: induced surface charges cancel the field inside — solid conductor shields fully, mesh leaks a little, insulator not at all.
electrostatic_shielding.hint: 1) Cage ON + solid conductor · 2) Switch to mesh and grow holes · 3) Try insulator / cage OFF

principle.desc: In electrostatic equilibrium, free charges on a hollow conductor rearrange until their field cancels any external field inside the cavity — E_inside = 0 for an ideal closed conductor (Faraday cage). A conducting mesh approximates this but lets some field leak through holes (worse as holes grow). An insulator has no free charges to rearrange, so it does not shield.
principle.equation: E_{inside} = 0 \; (\text{ideal closed conductor});; E_{inside} = E_0 / S(\text{material},\,\text{hole size})
principle.observe: Solid: lines end on the cage with induced +/−. Mesh: leak through holes. Insulator/OFF: lines go straight through.

controls.title: Faraday cage lab
controls.E0Help: The uniform field approaching the cage from outside.
controls.holeMmHelp: Only affects the mesh material — smaller holes shield better.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: A solid conductor in electrostatic equilibrium has zero field inside any cavity it encloses — induced surface charges cancel the external field exactly.
teach.t2: A conducting mesh approximates a solid shell but leaks field through its gaps; shielding improves as hole size shrinks relative to the cage.
teach.t3: An insulator has no free charges to redistribute, so it provides no shielding — the external field passes through essentially unchanged.
teach.t4: Real Faraday cages: a car body during a lightning strike, MRI room shielding, and braided/foil shields around cables.

electrospray_spinning.title: Electrostatic Spraying and Spinning
electrospray_spinning.desc: Nozzle at high voltage vs grounded collector: above onset the meniscus forms a Taylor cone — low-viscosity liquids electrospray into charged droplets, high-viscosity liquids electrospin into a continuous nanofiber.
electrospray_spinning.hint: 1) Raise V past onset · 2) Toggle low η (spray) vs high η (spin) · 3) Check Rayleigh limit vs droplet size

principle.desc: A liquid at a high-voltage nozzle faces a grounded collector. Above an onset voltage the meniscus becomes a Taylor cone and a thin jet is drawn out. Low-viscosity liquids cannot hold a continuous jet — it breaks into charged droplets that mutually repel (electrospray / coatings). High-viscosity polymer solutions resist breakup; the jet whips and stretches into a nanofiber (electrospinning). A droplet cannot carry more charge than the Rayleigh limit without fissioning.
principle.observe: Gold marker on the Rayleigh curve. Below the nozzle: droplet fan (spray) or whipping fiber (spin).

controls.title: Electrospray lab
controls.voltageHelp: Raise voltage above onset to form a Taylor cone and start jetting.
controls.dropletRadiusHelp: Sets the point marked on the Rayleigh charge-limit curve below.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Above the onset voltage, electric stress deforms the meniscus into a Taylor cone and draws out a thin jet.
teach.t2: Low-viscosity liquids cannot sustain a continuous jet — it breaks into droplets that mutually repel (electrospray), giving a self-dispersing, more uniform spray.
teach.t3: High-viscosity polymer solutions resist breakup; the jet instead whips and stretches into one continuous nanofiber (electrospinning), used for filters and tissue scaffolds.
teach.t4: A droplet fissions once its charge exceeds the Rayleigh limit q_R = 8π√(ε₀γR³), where Coulomb repulsion overcomes surface tension.

electrostatic_precipitator.title: Electrostatic Precipitator
electrostatic_precipitator.desc: Corona wire charges dust, field drifts it onto grounded plates: Deutsch-Anderson collection efficiency vs particle size.
electrostatic_precipitator.hint: 1) Raise voltage (stronger E,w) · 2) Change particle size · 3) Slow the gas · watch η and plate piles

principle.desc: An ESP cleans gas in three steps. (1) Charge: a thin HV wire runs corona and ions attach to dust. (2) Drift: the electric field pulls charged particles sideways to grounded plates (drift speed w balances qE against Stokes drag). (3) Collect: dust sticks on the plates; clean gas exits. Collection efficiency follows Deutsch–Anderson: η = 1 − exp(−wA/Q). Larger w, more plate area A, or smaller flow Q all raise η.
principle.observe: Switch the field Off to see dust drift straight through uncollected; switch it On to see it charge and pile on the plates.

controls.title: Precipitator lab
controls.voltageHelp: Raise V to strengthen the field and speed up drift (only while the field is On).
controls.radiusHelp: Charge grows as r², drag grows as r — drift velocity w scales with r.
controls.velocityHelp: Faster gas flow means less time in the duct to drift onto a plate.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Three steps: corona charging of dust, electric-field drift toward a plate, and collection where it sticks.
teach.t2: Drift velocity w = qE/(6πμr) balances electric force against Stokes drag.
teach.t3: Deutsch-Anderson equation η = 1 − e^(−wA/Q): more plate area or slower flow both raise efficiency.
teach.t4: Higher voltage raises E and w, raising η; plates are periodically rapped to shake collected dust into a hopper.

micro_electrokinetics.title: Micro-Electrokinetic Systems
micro_electrokinetics.desc: Electrophoresis, electroosmosis, and dielectrophoresis in microfluidics — particle drift, plug flow, and field-gradient forces on lab-on-a-chip scales.
micro_electrokinetics.hint: 1) Pick a mode · 2) Tune E / ζ / CM · 3) Compare what moves — the particle, the fluid, or a neutral bead in ∇E

principle.desc: Three related effects on chip scales. Electrophoresis (EP): a charged particle drifts through still fluid, v = εζ_p E/η. Electroosmosis (EO): the field drags the wall’s electric double layer, so the fluid itself plugs along (same formula with wall ζ) and carries particles with it. Dielectrophoresis (DEP): a neutral but polarizable particle in a non-uniform field feels F ∝ r³ Re[CM] ∇(E²) — toward high field if Re[CM] > 0, away if negative. Switch modes to run each experiment.
principle.observe: Animation redraws per mode. Gold marker = live point on the v or F curve.

controls.title: Electrokinetics lab
controls.fieldHelp: Applied electric field along the channel.
controls.zetaHelp: Sign sets drift/flow direction; magnitude sets speed.
controls.cmFactorHelp: Positive → drawn to high field; negative → repelled.
controls.radiusHelp: DEP force scales with the cube of particle radius.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Electrophoresis moves the charged particle itself through a stationary fluid; electroosmosis moves the bulk fluid (via the wall's double layer) and carries particles — even neutral ones — along with it.
teach.t2: Both electrophoresis and electroosmosis obey the same Smoluchowski relation v = εζE/η, just with a different zeta potential (particle vs. wall).
teach.t3: Dielectrophoresis needs no net charge on the particle, only a non-uniform field; the sign of the Clausius–Mossotti factor sets positive vs. negative DEP.
teach.t4: These effects underlie lab-on-a-chip tools: capillary electrophoresis for DNA/protein separation, electroosmotic micropumps, and DEP-based cell sorting.

meissner_effect.title: Meissner Effect — Perfect Diamagnetism
meissner_effect.desc: Below T_c a superconductor actively expels magnetic field via surface screening currents; field decays as B(x)=B0·e^(−x/λ_L); demo: magnet levitation.
meissner_effect.hint: 1) Cool below T_c · 2) Watch field expulsion + levitation · 3) Warm above T_c and see the magnet drop

principle.desc: Below T_c a Type-I superconductor is not just a perfect conductor — it actively expels magnetic flux from its bulk (Meissner effect) via persistent surface screening currents. That is true diamagnetism: the field that was present is pushed out, not frozen in. Just inside the surface, B decays as B(x) = B₀ e^{−x/λ_L} over the London depth λ_L. Above T_c the material is normal and field lines go straight through; a magnet resting on it will not levitate.
principle.observe: Below T_c: expelled field + hovering magnet. Above T_c: magnet down, field through.

controls.title: Meissner lab
controls.tempKHelp: Sweep across T_c to switch between superconducting and normal states.
controls.tcKHelp: Sets the transition point for this sample.
controls.lambdaNmHelp: Larger λ_L means the field penetrates deeper before being screened out.
controls.heightMmHelp: Only meaningful while superconducting — sets the levitation gap.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: The Meissner effect ≠ just zero resistance: a superconductor actively pushes field OUT of its bulk below T_c, regardless of field history.
teach.t2: The field is not blocked abruptly at the surface — it decays exponentially over the London penetration depth λ_L: B(x) = B₀e^(−x/λ_L).
teach.t3: At depth x = λ_L, the field has dropped to B₀/e ≈ 37% of its surface value.
teach.t4: Diamagnetic repulsion from screening currents is what levitates a magnet above a superconducting puck cooled below T_c — a classic demo, and the basis of maglev and quantum-locking tracks.

principle.desc: This is a classroom eddy-current brake: metal moving through a magnet gap. Changing flux makes closed current loops inside the plate.
