principle.steps:
Set a moderate B and thickness.
Raise plate speed — F_brake and power climb; look for INDUCTIVE BRAKING.
Increase σ or thickness at fixed speed — braking gets stronger.
Lower B toward zero — the brake nearly disappears.
principle.observe: Watch the plate, eddy loops, F_brake arrow, and the F vs v plot at the bottom.

controls.title: Eddy brake lab
controls.BHelp: Stronger gap field induces larger eddy currents for the same speed.
controls.thicknessHelp: Thicker conductors carry more eddy current and dissipate more power.
controls.sigmaHelp: Relative conductivity — copper-like materials brake harder than poor conductors.
controls.speedHelp: Plate speed through the gap in m/s. Braking and heating both grow with v.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Eddy currents are closed loops inside the bulk metal — not a single wire path.
teach.t2: Lenz’s law: the force on those currents opposes the motion (braking).
teach.t3: In this model, heating grows like σ B² v² t².
teach.t4: Real uses: roller-coaster brakes, train retarders, cooktops; laminated cores reduce unwanted eddy loss.

faraday_disc.title: Faraday Disc (Homopolar Generator)
faraday_disc.desc: A spinning metal disc in an axial B field makes a DC voltage between hub and rim. Connect a load to draw current.
faraday_disc.hint: 1) Set B · 2) Raise ω · 3) Set radius R and load R_load · read ε and I

principle.desc: This is Faraday’s disc — a homopolar generator. Spin the disc in an axial magnetic field. Charges feel a radial push, so a voltage appears between the hub brush and the rim brush. The open-circuit emf is ε = ½ B ω R². Close the circuit with R_load to get current I = ε / R_load.
principle.goal: Show that ε grows with B, ω, and R², and that I follows Ohm’s law through the load.
principle.steps:
Start with modest B and ω; note ε on the banner.
Double ω — ε should roughly double.
Increase R — watch the R² effect.
Lower R_load — I rises while ε stays the same (ideal source).
principle.observe: Watch the spinning disc, hub/rim brushes, load resistor, and the ε vs ω plot.

controls.title: Homopolar lab
controls.BHelp: Uniform field along the disc axis.
controls.RHelp: Outer radius from hub brush to rim brush.
controls.RloadHelp: External resistance closing the hub–rim circuit.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Homopolar generators make DC without a commutator — polarity stays fixed.
teach.t2: ε = ½ B ω R² comes from integrating (v×B)·dr from hub to rim.
teach.t3: You need brushes at hub and rim; the disc alone is not a closed circuit.
teach.t4: Historically important: motional emf without an obvious changing-flux loop.

ac_power_factor.title: AC Power Factor & Phasors
ac_power_factor.desc: An AC motor load makes current lag voltage. Real power P falls as the lag angle φ grows.
ac_power_factor.hint: 1) Set V_rms and I_rms · 2) Sweep φ (lag only) · 3) Watch P, Q, S and cos φ

principle.desc: This is a wattmeter bench for an inductive motor on AC. Current lags voltage by angle φ (lag only in this lab). Real power is P = VI cosφ. Reactive power is Q = VI sinφ. Apparent power is S = VI. Power factor is cosφ. Small φ means good PF; large lag means poor PF.
principle.equation: P=V I\cos\phi\quad\cdot\quad Q=V I\sin\phi\quad\cdot\quad S=VI\quad\cdot\quad PF=\cos\phi
principle.goal: Connect the lag angle φ to P, Q, S, and the power factor.
principle.steps:
Set φ near 0° — look for GOOD POWER FACTOR.
Raise φ toward 80° — P falls, Q rises, S stays V·I.
Watch the phasor meter: I lags V.
principle.observe: AC source → wattmeter → motor, plus phasor meter and the power triangle.

controls.title: Power-factor lab
controls.IrmsHelp: RMS current drawn by the load.
controls.phiHelp: Lag angle of current behind voltage (degrees). This slider is lag-only (motor-like).

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: S is the full VI product; only the in-phase part P does useful average work.
teach.t2: PF = cosφ = P/S. Poor PF still loads wires and generators with full S.
teach.t3: Motors lag. Factories often add capacitors to improve PF.
teach.t4: The power triangle makes P² + Q² = S² easy to see.

rotating_magnetic_field.title: Three-Phase Rotating Magnetic Field
rotating_magnetic_field.desc: Three stator coils 120° apart make a magnetic field that spins at supply frequency — the heart of an induction motor.
rotating_magnetic_field.hint: 1) Set frequency · 2) Set B₀ · 3) Toggle phase components On/Off · watch B_rot and the rotor

principle.desc: This is a three-phase stator like in an induction motor. Three windings (Phase A, B, C) sit 120° apart. Their fields add to one rotating vector of size about 1.5 B₀. That spinning field is what turns the rotor.
principle.goal: See three phase fields combine into one rotating resultant of nearly constant length.
principle.steps:
Turn phase components On — watch A, B, C oscillate.
Turn them Off — only B_rot remains; watch its tip trail a circle.
Raise f — rotation speeds up.
Change B₀ — check |B_rot| ≈ 1.5 B₀.
principle.observe: Stator ring, Phase A/B/C coils, rotor bar, and the circular tip trail of B_rot.

controls.title: RMF lab
controls.freqHelp: Electrical frequency; the field rotates at this rate.
controls.B0Help: Peak field from each phase winding (tesla).
controls.showComponentsHelp: Show or hide the three oscillating phase vectors.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: One phase makes a pulsing field; three phases make a rotating field.
teach.t2: Ideal |B| ≈ 1.5 B₀ when phases are balanced and 120° apart.
teach.t3: Swap any two phase wires and the field spins the other way.
teach.t4: Induction motors chase this field; slip between field and rotor sets torque.

forced_em_resonance.title: Forced RLC Resonance
forced_em_resonance.desc: Drive a series RLC with a function generator. Current peaks at f₀; smaller R makes a taller, sharper peak.
forced_em_resonance.hint: 1) Set L and C to fix f₀ · 2) Sweep drive f · 3) Lower R to raise Q — watch the peak

principle.desc: This is a forced-resonance lab bench: function generator → series R, L, C → ammeter. Impedance is lowest at f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)), so current peaks. Quality factor Q rises when R falls — the peak gets taller and narrower.
principle.goal: Tune drive frequency through f₀ and see how R, L, and C shape the current peak.
principle.steps:
Note f₀ from L and C.
Sweep f across f₀ — look for ★ ON RESONANCE and a current peak.
Lower R — peak rises and narrows (higher Q).
Change C or L and watch f₀ move.
principle.observe: Function generator, RLC parts, ammeter reading, and the I vs f curve.

controls.title: RLC drive lab
controls.RHelp: Series resistance — smaller R means higher Q and a taller, narrower peak.
controls.CHelp: Series capacitance; with L it sets f₀.
controls.fHelp: Generator frequency; resonance when f ≈ f₀.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: At resonance, ωL = 1/(ωC), so Z = R and current is V/R.
teach.t2: Below f₀ the circuit looks capacitive; above f₀ it looks inductive.
teach.t3: High Q means a sharp I(f) peak — useful for filters and tuning.
teach.t4: Same idea as radio tuners and other driven oscillators.

em_wave_radiation.title: Dipole EM Wave Radiation
em_wave_radiation.desc: A short dipole on an RF feed radiates EM waves; frequency sets λ, and the figure-8 pattern is brightest broadside with nulls on the wire axis.
em_wave_radiation.hint: 1) Set frequency (MHz) · 2) Raise amplitude · 3) Toggle near/far · look for figure-8 lobes and axis nulls

principle.desc: Only accelerating charge radiates. A short dipole driven by an RF feed launches waves with λ = c/f. In the far field the power pattern is ~ sin²θ: strongest broadside, zero along the wire. The radiation zone starts roughly beyond r ~ λ. Raise amplitude to see stronger expanding fronts.
principle.goal: Connect frequency to λ and see that energy goes broadside — not along the antenna wire.
principle.steps:
Raise frequency — λ shrinks (ruler between fronts).
Raise amplitude until you see RADIATING.
Toggle near/far to mark the radiation zone.
principle.observe: 2D: short dipole + RF feed, λ ruler, figure-8 plot. 3D: expanding wavefronts.

controls.title: Radiation lab
controls.frequencyHelp: RF drive frequency of the short dipole; sets λ = c/f (shown in MHz on the scene).
controls.amplitudeHelp: Dipole strength — turn this up until the green RADIATING banner appears.
controls.showNearFarHelp: Dashed ring: approximate start of the far-field radiation zone.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Static charges do not radiate; radiation needs acceleration (time-varying currents/dipoles).
teach.t2: In the far field, E and B are transverse and travel together as an EM wave at c.
teach.t3: Dipole pattern: strongest broadside (θ = 90°), null along the dipole axis.
teach.t4: Antennas, radio, and light all share this same radiated-wave physics at different frequencies.

em_wave_refraction.title: EM Wave Refraction (Snell)
em_wave_refraction.desc: At a dielectric interface (try air→glass), rays bend by Snell’s law; past the critical angle you get total internal reflection.
em_wave_refraction.hint: 1) Set n₁ & n₂ (air→glass ≈ 1 / 1.5) · 2) Sweep θ₁ · 3) Watch θ₂ arcs and TIR banner

principle.desc: Snell’s law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. Medium 1 and Medium 2 meet at a flat interface. When n₁ > n₂ and θ₁ exceeds the critical angle, there is no real θ₂ — total internal reflection (TIR). A Snell check near zero means the refracted ray is consistent.
principle.goal: Get a green REFRACTION OK state, then push into TIR and find θ_c on the plot.
principle.steps:
Start n₁≈1, n₂≈1.5 (air→glass) and raise θ₁ — θ₂ stays smaller.
Flip to n₁ > n₂ and raise θ₁ until the red TIR banner appears.
Read θ_c on the bottom plot (amber line).
principle.observe: 2D: labeled media, θ₁/θ₂ arcs, Snell check, TIR banner. 3D: interface rays.

controls.title: Snell lab
controls.theta1Help: Angle from the surface normal in Medium 1 — turn this to bend or hit TIR.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Snell’s law is phase matching along the boundary — the same physics for light and radio waves.
teach.t2: Critical angle exists only when n₁ > n₂; beyond it, energy reflects (evanescent field still exists).
teach.t3: Fresnel R depends on angle and polarization; this lab shows a teaching s-polarized scale.
teach.t4: Fiber optics, prisms, and radar ground bounce all use refraction and TIR at interfaces.

radar_principles.title: Pulse Radar Principles
radar_principles.desc: A TX dish pulses a target; delay gives range R = cτ/2. PRF too high (or R too far) makes the range ambiguous.
radar_principles.hint: 1) Set pulse width (µs) & PRF · 2) Place target range · 3) Aim for green RANGE LOCKED

principle.desc: Pulse radar: TX dish sends a short burst; echo delay τ clocks the two-way trip so R = cτ/2. Unambiguous range shrinks if PRF is high. Short pulses give finer range resolution. Echo power falls steeply with range (∼σ/R⁴).
principle.goal: Lock a clean range on the A-scope, then break it into AMBIGUOUS by raising PRF.
principle.steps:
Put the target inside R_unamb — expect RANGE LOCKED.
Raise PRF until the banner flips to AMBIGUOUS.
Shorten the pulse — ΔR improves (finer range bins).
Raise σ or shrink R — stronger echo on the A-scope.
principle.observe: 2D: TX dish, target, km path, A-scope time axis, Pr(R). 3D: pulse out and return.

controls.title: Pulse radar lab
controls.pulseWidthHelp: Transmit pulse duration (slider in seconds; scene shows µs). Shorter → finer ΔR.
controls.prfHelp: Pulses per second — too high and far targets become AMBIGUOUS.
controls.rangeHelp: One-way distance to the target (shown in km on the flight path).
controls.sigmaHelp: How strongly the target reflects (radar cross-section).

info.ambiguous: AMBIGUOUS (PRF too high / R too far)

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Time of flight measures range: every microsecond of delay is about 150 m one-way.
teach.t2: PRF sets how often you listen — too high and far echoes wrap into the next interval.
teach.t3: Short pulses give fine ΔR but carry less energy unless peak power rises.
teach.t4: Received power plummets with range (∼1/R⁴) — big antennas and high peak power fight that loss.

stealth_technology.title: Stealth & Radar Cross-Section
stealth_technology.desc: Pick a stealth shape class. The same radar illuminates a conventional airframe and that stealth geometry; catalog σ_eff (m²) is the teaching-scale frontal RCS.
stealth_technology.hint: 1) Choose a stealth shape · 2) Read catalog σ_eff (m²) · 3) Optional RAM / f · 4) Click the dish or a jet (3D)

principle.desc: RCS is how big the echo looks to the radar. Each stealth class has a catalog frontal σ_eff in m² (faceted, blended, flying wing, cruise/UAV). RAM slightly lowers that value; long λ (low f) adds diffraction. Remaining RCS % = σ_stealth / σ_conventional.
principle.goal: Select a shape and compare its real σ_eff (m²) with the conventional baseline.
principle.steps:
Pick Faceted, Blended, Flying wing, or Cruise/UAV.
Read catalog σ_eff in m² for that class.
Optional RAM lowers σ_eff a little more.
Lower frequency — diffraction hint rises (geometric stealth less perfect).
principle.observe: 2D: radar dish aiming at conventional vs the selected stealth silhouette, σ_eff in m². 3D: reduced return lobes.

controls.title: RCS stealth lab
controls.shapeHelp: Pick a stealth geometry. σ_eff is the teaching-scale frontal RCS (m²) for that class at X-band.
controls.absorbHelp: Extra RAM on top of the shape’s catalog RCS. 0 = catalog σ_eff.
controls.frequencyHelp: Carrier frequency (scene shows GHz). Lower f → longer λ → more diffraction.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Shaping aims specular reflections away from the threat radar — facets and smooth blends matter.
teach.t2: RAM (radar-absorbent material) trades reflected power for heat inside the coating.
teach.t3: Remaining RCS % shows how much of the conventional echo is left.
teach.t4: At long λ (low f), edges diffract and cavities resonate — perfect geometric stealth fails.

microwave_oven.title: Microwave Oven Cavity
microwave_oven.desc: A magnetron feeds a cavity through a waveguide; hot antinodes and cold nodes heat food — turntable On averages them.
microwave_oven.hint: 1) Set power · 2) Pick mode · 3) Turntable On/Off · 4) Raise water % — look for HEATING

principle.desc: Magnetron ≈ 2.45 GHz → waveguide → metal cavity. Standing waves make hot antinodes and cold nodes. Water absorbs microwave power. Turntable On averages hot/cold spots so food cooks more evenly; Off leaves fixed cold spots.
principle.goal: See HEATING, then compare turntable On (averaging) vs Off (uneven).
principle.steps:
Note 2.45 GHz and free-space λ.
Change mode index — node count and |E| plot change.
Set Turntable On — spots smear; Off — cold spots stay put.
Raise water % — heating proxy rises.
principle.observe: 2D: oven box, door mesh, magnetron, waveguide, food on turntable. 3D: cavity glow.

controls.title: Oven cavity lab
controls.powerHelp: Power into the cavity — raise until the green HEATING banner appears.
controls.turntableHelp: On = food rotates and averages hot/cold spots. Off = food sits still — cold nodes stay cold.
controls.waterFracHelp: Water content of the food (shown as %). More water → more heating.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: 2.45 GHz is in an ISM band where water absorbs efficiently and the cavity size is practical.
teach.t2: Metal walls enforce boundary conditions → discrete cavity modes and standing waves.
teach.t3: Nodes are cold; antinodes are hot — turntables (or mode stirrers) improve uniformity.
teach.t4: Heating is dielectric loss in polar molecules, not “radioactive” and not uniform like a conventional oven.

mechanical_equilibrium.title: Stable & Unstable Equilibrium
mechanical_equilibrium.desc: Same kick, two landscapes: a valley restores (V″>0) while a hill runs away (V″<0). Dual 2D|3D marble lab.
mechanical_equilibrium.hint: 1) Nudge both marbles · 2) Watch the valley oscillate · 3) Watch the hill fall · 4) Raise k or damping

principle.desc: Equilibrium means net force is zero. Stability is about the curvature of the potential. In a valley, a small displacement creates a restoring force F=−kx. On a hill, the force points further downhill. Neutral balance (flat V) is the in-between case.
principle.goal: Give both systems the same nudge and see restoration vs runaway.
principle.steps:
Press Nudge — both marbles get a kick.
The green valley oscillates and settles.
The red hill leaves the peak.
Raise stiffness k — the well oscillates faster; the hill still runs away.
principle.observe: 2D: valley vs hill plus V(x) plot. 3D: bowl vs inverted hill. Green force arrows show F=−∇V.

controls.title: Equilibrium lab
controls.kHelp: Curvature of V. Larger k → stronger restoring (or stronger runaway) force.
controls.dampHelp: Friction-like term. Helps the valley settle; barely saves the hill.
controls.kickHelp: Impulse applied to both marbles when you press Nudge.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: Equilibrium: F=0. Stability: what happens after a tiny push.
teach.t2: Stable ⇔ local minimum of V (V″>0). Unstable ⇔ local maximum (V″<0).
teach.t3: The same idea appears in nuclei: the fission saddle is an unstable direction on the energy surface.

bowl.title: Stable well
bowl.desc: Any small slide comes back. V″>0 at the bottom.

hill.title: Unstable hill
hill.desc: Balanced only at the peak. A nudge runs away.

fission_mechanism.title: Fission Mechanism — Liquid Drop to Scission
fission_mechanism.desc: Watch one nucleus: neutron capture, compound wobble, elongation over the saddle, scission, fragments + neutrons.
fission_mechanism.hint: 1) Pick U-235 / U-238 / Pu-239 · 2) Set neutron energy · 3) Thermal vs Fast · 4) Watch the barrier plot

principle.desc: Fission is a shape change of a charged liquid drop. A captured neutron forms a hot compound nucleus. If excitation beats the fission barrier, the drop elongates through a saddle, a neck pinches off (scission), and Coulomb repulsion flings two fragments apart — plus ~2.5 neutrons and ~200 MeV.
principle.goal: See why thermal neutrons fission U-235 but U-238 needs a fast neutron.
principle.steps:
Start with U-235 and Thermal (0.025 MeV) — the path opens.
Switch to U-238 at the same energy — the barrier holds.
Press Fast (~2 MeV) — U-238 can go over the saddle too.
Watch β (deformation) climb the barrier plot.
principle.observe: Left: liquid-drop cartoon. Right: schematic V(β). Green marker = over the saddle.

controls.title: Mechanism lab
controls.energyHelp: Thermal ~0.025 MeV. Fast fission needs a few MeV, especially for U-238.
controls.speedHelp: How fast the capture→scission cycle plays.

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: U-235 (and Pu-239) can fission with a slow neutron; U-238 generally cannot.
teach.t2: The barrier is a saddle in deformation energy: surface energy vs Coulomb energy.
teach.t3: Scission is the instant the neck breaks; fragments then fly apart on Coulomb repulsion.
teach.t4: This lab is one nucleus. The chain-reaction grid is the separate Nuclear Fission experiment.

drop.title: Liquid drop
drop.desc: Nucleons held by the strong force, pushed apart by charge. Shape is the whole story.

atomic_bomb.title: Atomic Bomb — Gun, Implosion, Boosted Fission
atomic_bomb.desc: Watch neutrons leak or multiply. Gun-type joins two pieces; implosion squeezes a pit; boosted adds extra neutrons.
atomic_bomb.hint: Pick a type. Watch blue neutrons. k < 1 they leak. k > 1 they multiply.

principle.desc: A nuclear explosion needs a mass to become supercritical (k_eff>1) faster than neutrons can leak or predetonate. Gun-type slams two subcritical HEU pieces together. Implosion squeezes a plutonium pit so density (and k) jump. Fusion-boosted fission puts D–T in the pit: fusion neutrons raise the fission completeness. These are public historical concepts — not a design guide.
principle.goal: See how each assembly method drives k_eff through 1, and why implosion/boost differ from the gun.
principle.steps:
Run Gun-type — two pieces meet; k_eff rises.
Lower assembly speed — the k≈1 window lasts longer (predetonation teaching note).
Switch to Implosion — compression raises k more sharply.
Switch to Boosted — D–T core adds extra neutrons near the end.
principle.observe: 2D schematic + k_eff curve. 3D: tube (gun) or lens-sphere (implosion). Yield number is a toy proxy, not a real yield.

controls.title: Assembly lab
controls.typeHelp: Gun-type (Little Boy class), implosion (Fat Man class), fusion-boosted fission.
controls.speedHelp: Faster assembly shortens the time spent near k≈1 (gun-type teaching).
controls.compressHelp: Implosion density factor in the toy model. Higher → larger k_eff.
controls.boostHelp: How strongly D–T fusion neutrons help fission the pit (boosted type).

teach.title: Key ideas
teach.t1: k is simple: neutrons next generation ÷ neutrons now. Below 1 the chain dies. Above 1 it grows.
teach.t2: Gun-type: two pieces that are each too small. Slide them into one piece so fewer neutrons leak.
teach.t3: Implosion: squeeze the pit. Denser means more hits, so k jumps. Boosted: extra neutrons from D–T — still a fission bomb.
teach.t4: This is a public teaching cartoon, not a design. The yield number is not real.

bullet.title: Projectile mass
bullet.desc: A subcritical HEU piece fired toward the target piece.

target.title: Target mass
target.desc: Second subcritical piece. Together they can go supercritical.

pit.title: Fissile pit
pit.desc: Schematic plutonium core compressed by the lenses.

core.title: D–T boost
core.desc: Fusion neutrons (schematic) help fission the pit more completely.

ai.title: AI — Neural Wavefunction
ai.desc: A neural network learns this orbital's radial probability P(r) = r²R(r)² by gradient descent — watch it converge to the exact quantum solution.
ai.how:
The AI is a small neural network: it takes a radius r and outputs the wavefunction value there.
At first its weights are random, so its curve (magenta) is nonsense.
Each step it measures how far its curve is from the exact quantum answer (the 'loss') and nudges every weight to shrink that error — this is gradient descent.
After enough steps the network's curve lands on the true wavefunction: it has learned the orbital. This is exactly how neural networks are trained, shown live.
